chapter_evidence.title: Why Each One Should Eat His Own Turtles: Equality in Uncertainty
chapter_evidence.hook: A bad turtle dinner tells you more about fairness than a hundred polished disclosure forms.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Helpful advice can be dirtier than open selling. The test is not warmth or honesty in tone; it is whether the person steering your choice will carry the loss with you.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Trust a recommendation only after you know whether the person making it will share the downside if it goes wrong.
chapter_evidence.try: Before accepting one live recommendation today, write three names: who gains now, who pays if it fails, and who would have to sign to share the loss.
extracts: The simplest unfairness is not hidden in a contract.
The other side is being fed turtles.
You just do not get to leave the bad meal on someone else's plate and call the handoff help.
examples: Mathieu asks for the refund term
Grace slides over the co-investment form
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Learn to test advice by exposure, not by tone. Before you accept a recommendation, identify who benefits immediately and who pays if the hidden risk appears later. The cleaner choice either shares the downside or makes the asymmetry visible enough to price.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Take one recommendation you are considering and write a three-column ledger: upside holder, downside holder, and one change that would make the exposure shared.

chapter_evidence.title: The Most Intolerant Wins: The Dominance of the Stubborn Minority
chapter_evidence.hook: One tiny mark on a lemonade bottle can move an entire shelf without asking the crowd to care.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The strict side does not need to persuade the flexible side. It only needs a default the flexible side can tolerate while the strict side cannot tolerate the alternative.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A small minority can rule when its constraint is hard and the majority can live with the stricter option.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one group choice near you and mark which side can accept both options, which side can accept only one, and where a local rule becomes the default.
extracts: Sophie looks at the meeting agenda in Brussels and hears three side conversations in French before the regulatory analyst has finished reading the product note.
A household adapts to one strict member.
Social change sometimes arrives this way: not through consensus, not through mass conversion, but through asymmetric tolerance finding a channel.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Learn to read group choices by tolerance, not only preference counts. The strict side gains leverage when its acceptable set is smaller and the flexible side can absorb the stricter default. Your job is to find the hard constraint and the channel that lets it scale.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Find one default near you, menu, meeting language, software setting, or building rule. Mark who strictly needs it and who merely tolerates it.

chapter_evidence.title: How to Legally Own Another Person
chapter_evidence.hook: The red pen pauses over one clause because a calendar can become a collar.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A person can be legally free and still be practically owned. The leash is whatever he cannot afford to lose: salary, school fees, references, status, or future work.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Practical freedom depends on what you can refuse without losing the future you need.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one obligation you call voluntary and list the three things you would lose by refusing it. Circle the one that actually governs your choice.
extracts: Marco smells disinfectant near the lab sink before he sees the failed sterilization line in the log.
The future does the threatening.
Practical freedom asks whether you can afford to walk through it.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Learn to test freedom by refusal cost. A person is not practically free merely because no one blocks the door. Practical freedom exists when refusal does not destroy the future the person needs.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one role you call free. Write down the job, person, or institution that can punish refusal, then name the exact thing it can take away.

chapter_evidence.title: The Skin of Others in Your Game
chapter_evidence.hook: The benefits card sits beside the safety report because courage can spend a family's money first.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Truth can look like a private choice until the bill reaches a spouse, a grant team, a brother's job, or a child's insurance. The first task is to find those hidden passengers.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Before you judge silence or courage, map the people nearby who would absorb retaliation; truth-telling is cleaner when its hidden passengers are protected.
chapter_evidence.try: Take one live objection you are delaying and write three names or groups that would pay first if you spoke. Add the one protection they need before you decide.
extracts: Julien opens the retaining-wall photo on his tablet and sees the crack running through the concrete like a dark thread.
First.
Courage becomes cleaner when the bill lands closer to the person who earned it.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Before calling a choice brave or cowardly, identify the people who would pay first. The skill is to move pressure into the open, then design the action so retaliation lands closer to the person who created the harm.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one postponed objection. In five lines, name the hidden passengers, the evidence, the retaliation path, the protection needed, and the first person to notify.

chapter_evidence.title: Life in the Simulation Machine
chapter_evidence.hook: Slush at the curb proves the turn lane only works on the screen.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Models become dangerous not when they simplify, but when their errors are paid by people outside the model and reality cannot overrule the diagram.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Make every abstraction prove where it touches reality, then give the people who carry model error enough authority to stop the decision.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one forecast you trust and name the exact place where it should be watched in use. Add who can halt the plan if reality contradicts it.
extracts: Ingrid stands under the blue light over the triage desk while the staffing forecast sits open on a tablet.
A model is a compression.
Abstraction becomes safer when it is forced to report to the place where its mistakes land, especially when the clean forecast has no scar from past failures.
examples: Emily watches the truck swing wide
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use models as proposals, not verdicts. Before trusting one, identify where it touches reality, who absorbs the error, and what observation would force a change.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one model-backed decision. Find one person who would carry the error and ask what field condition the model is missing.

chapter_evidence.title: The Intellectual Yet Idiot
chapter_evidence.hook: Soil on one cuff tells the farm panel what the agenda forgot to ask.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The credential is not the danger. The danger is advice that collects status from being elegant while farmers, nurses, riders, students, or retirees pay for the miss.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Trust expertise more when it is exposed to correction, and discount it when credentialed distance lets the adviser keep upside while others carry error.
chapter_evidence.try: Before taking expert advice today, ask what personal loss would correct the adviser if the advice fails. If none appears, find the nearest practitioner loop.
extracts: Maja's tote is speckled with rain when she meets the remote advisor outside the clinic.
The grower mentions rain timing.
The more insulated the expert is from the cost of error, the more you should demand practitioner knowledge before turning theory into power.
examples: Laura asks who loses a crop
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Do not accept or reject expertise by status alone. Rank advice by its correction loop: who pays for error, who can update the claim, and whether practitioners can challenge the theory before it becomes power.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Take one recommendation you received. Write the adviser's credential, the practitioner's correction loop, and the downside each person would feel if wrong.

chapter_evidence.title: Inequality and Skin in the Game
chapter_evidence.hook: Bonus schedules look different when the losses have already been handed to everyone else.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Unequal rewards are not automatically corrupt, but they become harder to defend when winners collect upside after exporting the risks that created it.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Judge inequality by exposure: rewards deserve more respect when winners can fall from the same risks they ask others to bear.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one hierarchy you accept or resent. Write who gets the upside, who can fall, and what clause would make reward and loss travel together.
extracts: "We recommend decisive cuts," the fund partner says while Giulia looks at the cap table projected on the wall.
Petra asks who answers when the freezer fails before accepting the veto.
Inequality becomes more defensible when the winners cannot export the downside.
examples: Giulia asks the fund to stay in
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: When you see unequal reward, do not stop at the size of the gap. Trace whether the people receiving the upside can also fall from the risk that created it.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Review one bonus, fee, subsidy, or authority right. Write the upside path, the downside path, and one clause that would reconnect them.

chapter_evidence.title: An Expert Called Lindy
chapter_evidence.hook: Worn cloth spines under the scanner may know more than the glossy new shelf.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Launch claims and antique aura both skip the same test: repeated stress. Endurance matters when it records pressure that a fresh pitch has not faced.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Use endurance as evidence under uncertainty, but respect old things only when survival shows repeated usefulness instead of antique charm.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one tool you are about to replace. Check its survival record: failures endured, requests repeated, repairs made, and stress the newcomer has not met.
extracts: Starter bubbles under a glass lid while Marit lines up three test loaves from the viral method.
The old method does not win because it is romantic.
It is not a king.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use endurance as a credibility signal when uncertainty is high. Separate genuine survival under stress from mere age, monopoly, or nostalgia.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one old process on your desk. Write the last three stresses it survived and one stress the replacement has not yet faced.

chapter_evidence.title: Surgeons Should Not Look like Surgeons
chapter_evidence.hook: A paper gown on the chair can make bedside polish feel more important than the hand record.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Polish can be useful manners, but it becomes dangerous when it substitutes for the evidence that matters under risk: volume, records, repairs, trials, and outcomes.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Do not reject polish; demote it until practical signals show the person can perform when consequences are real.
chapter_evidence.try: Before trusting one polished signal today, ask for the performance record behind it: volume, error rate, repeat use, customer retention, or field trial.
extracts: "He presents beautifully," the partner says as Anke slides transcript pages under a brass lamp.
Ask yourself what the polished signal is allowed to hide.
When the stakes are real, costume should introduce the evidence, not replace it.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use polish as a weak signal and performance records as strong signals. The higher the stakes, the closer your evidence should be to the place where the person can fail.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one polished signal that recently influenced you. Find the closest performance record behind it and write whether the record confirms or weakens trust.

chapter_evidence.title: Only the Rich Are Poisoned: The Preferences of Others
chapter_evidence.hook: A split cork beside a plain plate can expose a desire the label created.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Money does not poison taste by buying nice things. It poisons taste when status vendors can sell you desires that never came from use.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Protect autonomy by testing preferences against direct use before status pressure turns someone else's taste into your obligation.
chapter_evidence.try: Take one expensive preference you are considering and test it in ordinary use. Hide the brand, lower the audience, and ask whether you still want it.
extracts: Mud flakes below the linen bench while Sofia studies the designer's photo mockup.
This is how preference gets outsourced.
A preference is yours when it survives use without needing an audience to hold it up.
examples: Vincent ranks the school day second
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Before adopting a desire, check whether it came from use or from status pressure. The goal is not austerity; it is autonomy over what you actually want.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one desired purchase or commitment. Remove the audience and run one direct-use test before deciding whether the desire is yours.

chapter_evidence.title: Facta non Verba (Deeds Before Words)
chapter_evidence.hook: A red failed-test icon can tell more truth than an hour of safety values.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Sincerity is easiest to fake where words cost nothing. The better audit asks what changed in behavior when the statement became expensive.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: When words are cheap, trust the paid action: the test passed, the bus ridden, the ledger opened, the incentive changed.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one value you recently stated. Find the next costly action that would prove it, then schedule or do that action before repeating the words.
extracts: "Transparency is one of our values," the director says while Isabel turns a board packet clipped with a binder ring.
The wellness policy that never changes promotion evidence?
It is an evidence rule for sincerity under consequence.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Treat words as a claim and costly behavior as evidence. The more trust a claim asks for, the more visible the deed should be.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Find one value you have said aloud. Attach one costly behavior to it today, even if the cost is only time, convenience, or public visibility.

chapter_evidence.title: The Facts Are True, the News Is Fake
chapter_evidence.hook: A true clip beside a missing spreadsheet can still teach the wrong neighborhood.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A fact can be accurate and still mislead when selection, salience, and frame make it feel like the whole reality.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Before reacting to a packaged story, separate the raw event from the selection and frame that made it feel bigger or cleaner than reality.
chapter_evidence.try: Take one alarming item you saw today. Write the raw fact, the missing denominator or sequence, and the decision you would delay until both appear.
extracts: Locker doors flash in the paused hallway video while Paula lines up the timestamp log.
What is missing from the frame?
It is the pattern that remains when the frame is removed.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Treat vivid facts as starting points, not full maps. Rebuild scale, sequence, omissions, and direct records before allowing a packaged story to drive action.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Take one vivid item you almost shared. Add one missing context line, then decide whether it still deserves the same reaction.

chapter_evidence.title: The Merchandising of Virtue
chapter_evidence.hook: Fabric samples beside an ethics mockup can hide whose paycheck funds the applause.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A moral claim becomes suspect when praise and cost travel in opposite directions. Serious virtue is easier to trust when the claimant pays part of the bill.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Test virtue by tracing the invoice: moral language deserves more trust when reputational upside and real cost stay together.
chapter_evidence.try: Take one public moral claim you support. Write who gets praised, who pays, and one change that would move cost back toward the claimant.
extracts: Tomato skins stick to the stainless bin while Nina reads the window decal draft.
Put member budgets beside the group rule.
Virtue becomes less marketable and more serious when the cost cannot be hidden.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: When a moral claim appears, follow praise and cost separately. Trust rises when the claimant carries part of the cost and falls when the bill is moved to quieter people.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Find one virtue claim in your work or community. Write the praise line, the invoice line, and one way to make the claimant carry cost.

chapter_evidence.title: Peace, Neither Ink nor Blood
chapter_evidence.hook: Wet ink beside a floor map cannot keep a factory quiet by itself.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Peace is weakest when it depends on fresh signatures or exhausted tempers, but it lasts when each side can see the cost of breaking it tomorrow.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Judge peace by the lived consequence structure that keeps it stable after the ceremony ends and nobody feels noble anymore.
chapter_evidence.try: Find one agreement you rely on. Add the missing trigger, owner, consequence, or shared cost that would still work after goodwill fades.
extracts: Rubber gym mats are stacked after the pep rally when Hanna studies the handshake photo.
The practical rule is to design for the day after goodwill.
Peace becomes durable when the structure makes betrayal expensive and cooperation ordinary.
examples: Hanna gives the handshake a routine
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Treat calm and signatures as beginnings. Add triggers, records, and consequences that still work after goodwill fades.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one fragile agreement. Add one trigger, one record, and one consequence that would operate without another speech.

chapter_evidence.title: They Don't Know What They Are Talking About When They Talk About Religion
chapter_evidence.hook: A cooling meal tray can explain a fasting rule better than a paragraph about belief.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A belief system can be misread when outsiders treat it as a set of sentences. Practice shows what the rule does when people carry it with cost.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Interpret lived traditions through practice, risk, repetition, and function before reducing them to literal statements from outside.
chapter_evidence.try: Before judging one unfamiliar rule, ask what people do with it, when it costs them something, and what function it serves inside the group.
extracts: Calendar squares are marked in two colors when Léa Holm checks the deadline sheet.
They were incomplete without the practice.
You do not need to agree with every belief to avoid misreading a lived system as if it were only words.
examples: Léa asks what work violates the practice
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Before judging a belief system, move from literal statements to lived use. Watch what people repeat, risk, and protect through the practice.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one unfamiliar rule. Find one person or source that describes the practice in use, then write what function you missed at first glance.

chapter_evidence.title: No Worship Without Skin in the Game
chapter_evidence.hook: Orange cones before dawn reveal team commitment better than the captaincy speech.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Belief becomes visible not when it sounds sincere, but when it asks for surrendered time, comfort, money, status, or output.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Treat commitment as real when belief becomes cost-bearing practice, not when it merely decorates a statement or identity.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one belief you claim. Name the next concrete cost it asks from you, then pay a small version of that cost before discussing it again.
extracts: Refund envelopes line the table beside Julia Nilsen's laptop.
Which cost should count?
Serious worship means serious commitment with a visible cost close to the thing being worshipped, paid by the person making the claim.
examples: Emma waits on the captaincy vote
Noah asks for names beside nights
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Judge commitment by what it makes the believer give up. The closer the cost is to the claim, the more credible the belief becomes.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one belief you mention often. Pay one small cost for it today and write what the cost revealed about your actual commitment.

chapter_evidence.title: Is the Pope Atheist?
chapter_evidence.hook: Two yellow tabs on a budget sheet can test doctrine more sharply than a sermon.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The provocative question works only as a diagnostic. Declared belief becomes readable when an institution must pay to act as if the belief is true.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Read stated belief through behavior under exposure, especially when an institution must spend money, status, or convenience to live by it.
chapter_evidence.try: Take one stated belief in an organization you know. Find the budget line, access rule, or risk decision that would reveal whether it is carried as cost.
extracts: Paper programs fan across a banquet table while Clara Moreau watches the charity leader pray before donors.
Poor-first doctrine should protect aid when travel is comfortable.
The evidence is the cost the institution is willing to carry.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Treat stated belief as a claim, then look for institutional behavior where the claim costs money, status, access, convenience, or risk.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one institutional belief you hear often. Find the exact line, rule, or risk decision where it would become costly.

chapter_evidence.title: How to Be Rational About Rationality
chapter_evidence.hook: A laminated call tree can look messy and still beat the elegant evacuation app.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Rationality is not always the cleanest explanation, but in exposed life the rational practice is often the one that keeps people from ruin.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Judge rationality by survival under real constraints before dismissing messy beliefs, rituals, hedges, or habits as incoherent.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one habit that looks inefficient. Ask what error, ruin, or coordination failure it prevents before you replace it with a cleaner rule.
extracts: Lunchbox clasps snap shut while Mia Conti reads the family's food rule beside the allergy plan.
The rule is not efficient in the narrow sense.
It is behavior that keeps agents alive, solvent, coordinated, and able to continue under the conditions that actually correct them.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Before calling a practice irrational, identify what survival function it may serve. Then test that function where failure would actually hurt.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one messy rule you dislike. Write the ruin, error, or coordination failure it may prevent before proposing a cleaner replacement.

chapter_evidence.title: The Logic of Risk Taking
chapter_evidence.hook: A personal guarantee can make a growth story end with one bad quarter.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Good risk is not the one with the most exciting upside, but the one that preserves the right to keep playing after ordinary bad luck arrives.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Refuse risks whose downside can remove you from the game; survival is the condition that lets all future upside exist.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one attractive risk and write the worst case in one sentence. If that sentence ends future participation, redesign or refuse the deal.
extracts: "The quote is twenty percent cheaper," the buyer says while Eva Kowal looks at empty bins behind the pharmacy counter.
The rule is to separate risk from ruin.
The logic of risk taking is the logic of continued participation.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Before taking a risk, identify whether the worst case is survivable. Only then should upside, probability, and learning value enter the decision.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Take one attractive opportunity and write its ruin sentence. If the sentence ends participation, list one redesign that caps the downside.

chapter_evidence.title: An Optimistic Skeptic
chapter_evidence.hook: Bill Flack had no column, no publicist, and a better prediction record than most people who had both.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Confidence, fluency, and seniority feel like forecasting signals. They measure something real about a person's poise. What they do not measure is accuracy. The only signal that actually tracks accuracy is a checked record of past calls scored against outcomes.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Forecast credibility comes from tracked accuracy, not confidence or fluency. Respect limits where chaos defeats prediction, then work only questions where a record can be built.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one forecast you heard this week. Find that person's tracked record on past predictions in the same domain. Write one sentence on what you find. 'No record available' counts as an answer.
extracts: Ingrid manages vendor risk at a mid-size logistics company.
The receipt is not proof that you are right.
After six months, you will know whose predictions are worth your attention and whose are only worth your time while you are in the same room.
examples: Claire pulls two years of outcome logs before the routing vote
Sarah compares five years of vintage calls before committing barrels
Ingrid brings the outcome data before the curriculum vote
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Separate prestige signals from track-record evidence before acting on any prediction. When you hear a confident forecast, ask for the scored record before adjusting your estimate. When you make a forecast, write it as a number with a check date so it can be scored when outcomes arrive.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Find one prediction you made or heard in the last 24 hours about a project, client, or market outcome. Write it down with exact wording, a probability percentage, and a check date. This is the smallest unit of a score sheet.

chapter_evidence.title: Illusions of Knowledge
chapter_evidence.hook: Archie Cochrane spent forty years insisting that medicine test its confident claims. Then a specialist gave him a cancer verdict before the pathology results were back, and the verdict was wrong.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Explanatory overreach does not register as error; it arrives as clarity. The problem arrives precisely when your explanation is most convincing: before the evidence that would test it has come back.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: An explanation earns certainty when the evidence does, not when it sounds fluent. Before concluding, name what confirming evidence is still outstanding and mark the explanation as a candidate.
chapter_evidence.try: Take the next explanation you're about to give (to a colleague, client, or family member) and ask yourself one question before you say it: what piece of evidence, if it came back differently than expected, would change this explanation? If you cannot name that piece of evidence, your explanation has already closed before it should have. State it as provisional.
extracts: The question worth asking before you give your next explanation is not whether you might be wrong.
The explanation had not been lazy.
That sentence is the difference between a verdict and a candidate, and it is the only difference that matters before the evidence is in.
examples: Ben marks the crack memo provisional before the lab report files it as final
Petra gives the parents an explanation that closes before the assessment opens
The explanation arrives before the scan does, and parts get ordered
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Hold explanations in the register that matches the evidence behind them. Before any significant conclusion reaches a decision-maker, name the confirming evidence that is still outstanding, and mark the explanation as a candidate until that evidence returns.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Find one explanation you gave or received today (about a project, a decision, a person's behavior, or an outcome). Ask: had the confirming evidence actually returned by the time that explanation was offered? If not, how was the explanation's certainty level communicated? Note the gap.

chapter_evidence.title: Keeping Score
chapter_evidence.hook: When the CIA circulated a 1961 assessment using the phrase 'serious possibility,' Sherman Kent polled his colleagues on what it meant. Their estimates ranged from 20% to 80%. The same two words. The same document. Different numbers that implied completely different responses to the same threat.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A numerical probability feels like a communication tool. It is actually a diagnostic. Writing 55% instead of 'likely' forces you to confront what you actually believe before you can obscure it in language.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A verbal hedge survives because it can mean anything. A numerical probability forces the forecaster to commit to one claim, changing their own thinking before it changes anyone else's.
chapter_evidence.try: Find one claim you made in the last 48 hours using a hedge word: likely, probably, good chance, I think. Write down the specific percentage you actually believe. Then ask: could someone reading that percentage check it when the outcome arrives? If you would reinterpret the percentage after the fact, the number is not specific enough yet. Narrow it by 10 points.
extracts: Diego had been saying the company 'looks good' for three weeks when his partner slid a blank column across the deal memo and asked him to fill it in.
A record.
Both require the number.
examples: Hannah replaces 'likely' with 72% and finds that the number breaks the room's consensus
Diego fills in the blank column and finds the number contradicts three weeks of meetings
Camille replaces 'guarded prognosis' with 38% and finds the family had heard something much worse
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Replace verbal probability language with a specific number before any forecast leaves your hands. The number should be specific enough that you could not comfortably reinterpret it after the fact if the outcome differs from what you expected.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Find one verbal hedge you used today: likely, probably, good chance, I think. Write the specific percentage you actually meant. Then write the date when the outcome of this prediction will be knowable. Keep both numbers somewhere you will find them when that date arrives.

chapter_evidence.title: Superforecasters
chapter_evidence.hook: Staying on the hard question takes deliberate effort. The easier proxy arrives faster, generates the same feeling of analytical work, and produces an answer, which is exactly why it so often replaces the question you actually needed to answer.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Question substitution does not feel like taking a shortcut. The proxy question is genuinely difficult and the work feels real. The tell is that you have a confident answer ready and it covers the easier question, not the harder one you were supposed to answer.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Name the target question before any analysis, then check whether your conclusion addresses it or a simpler substitute. The error is invisible until you commit an answer.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one decision you are currently tracking: a project timeline, a negotiation outcome, a business forecast. Write down the exact question you are trying to answer, then write down the question you have actually been spending most time on. If they are different, you have already substituted. Rewrite your most recent estimate as an answer to the original question.
extracts: Kasia's debrief room had personality descriptors on the whiteboard.
The proxy question had told her the answer she expected.
If they differ, the work on the proxy may still be useful but it does not answer the target question, and presenting it as if it does is the last step in the substitution.
examples: David writes both questions side by side and finds his review only answers the easier one
Kasia's debrief room has personality traits on the whiteboard where outcome metrics should be
Hugo's referral rate is six times the base rate, which tells him he has been answering the wrong question
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Before doing analytical work on any significant decision, write the target question explicitly in one sentence. After completing the analysis, check whether your conclusion answers that sentence or a different one. If they do not match, mark the confidence level to reflect the proxy rather than the target.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Find one ongoing analysis or decision where you have a working conclusion. Write down the exact question you were supposed to answer. Then write down the question your conclusion actually answers. If they are different, note the gap and identify one piece of evidence that would address the target question rather than the proxy.

chapter_evidence.title: Supersmart?
chapter_evidence.hook: Enrico Fermi did not know how many piano tuners worked in Chicago. He built the number from smaller numbers he could estimate separately, and his answer was usually within a factor of two. That is not genius. That is method.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Breaking a big uncertain question into smaller uncertain parts feels like multiplying the uncertainty. It does not. Independent estimation errors partially cancel each other, and naming each component forces you to confront assumptions you would otherwise leave invisible.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Raw intelligence without a method produces brilliant-sounding wrong answers. Decompose the question into estimable parts, anchor each on the reference class, then adjust for what you know specifically.
chapter_evidence.try: Find one number you need to estimate this week: a project cost, a timeline, an audience size, a conversion rate. Before guessing, write three components the total is made of. Look up or estimate each component separately. Multiply or add them. Compare that number to your gut estimate. The gap between them is what decomposition is for.
extracts: Michael's board deck had 'TAM: $2.8B' on slide four.
His gut number was $2.8 billion.
The gut estimate has no such cancellation; its errors flow from a single judgment that can be confidently wrong in one direction by any amount.
examples: Michael's TAM decomposition comes back 40% below his gut number, and he uses it anyway
Frida's decomposed estimate runs 25 minutes long and changes the afternoon schedule
Aman anchors on four analogous cities before looking at local conditions, and the local factor shifts the estimate 18% upward
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: When estimating any uncertain quantity, break it into three or more components before producing a number. Anchor each component on the reference class (what happens in comparable cases) before adjusting for what you know specifically about this case.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Find one estimate you need to make today: a cost, a time, a count, a rate. Before producing the number, write three components it is made of. Estimate each component independently. Multiply or add them. Compare the result to what your gut said before you decomposed.

chapter_evidence.title: Superquants?
chapter_evidence.hook: Leon Panetta did not smooth the analysts' estimates into one number before taking them to the President. The probability that bin Laden was in the Abbottabad compound ranged from 40% to 95% across the senior analysts who had studied the same evidence. That spread was not a failure of analysis. It was the honest state of knowledge.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A probability range looks weaker than a single number. Decision-makers often press for the point estimate. But collapsing a range into a point does not reduce the uncertainty; it hides it. A calibrated range that separates what evidence has settled from what it has not yet reached is more useful to a decision-maker than a single number wearing false confidence.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Probabilistic honesty means distinguishing what evidence has settled from what it has not. Epistemic uncertainty shrinks with more data. Aleatory uncertainty does not, no matter how much you collect.
chapter_evidence.try: Take a probability you have stated recently: for a project, a decision, an outcome. Ask yourself: if you gathered ten times more data, would this probability narrow significantly? If yes, it is partly epistemic; name the data that would resolve it. If no, it is partly aleatory; your range is already as narrow as honest evidence allows. Restate the probability as a range rather than a point, and write next to it which component is which.
extracts: Barbara Mellers studied the forecasters who performed best in the Good Judgment Project and found something unexpected about their precision.
The range does not disappear.
It becomes implicit, unexamined, invisible to the people who most need to see it.
examples: James separates two types of uncertainty in interim trial data and the monitoring board reframes the stop decision
Manon refuses to give a yes/no on diversion and labels the two components in a 55-70% approach range
Niklas replaces a vague credit cover slide with a two-component default range and the committee sizes accordingly
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: When stating any probability, identify whether the uncertainty is epistemic (reducible with more evidence) or aleatory (irreducible regardless of more evidence). Express the estimate as a range that keeps both components visible rather than collapsing them into a single point that hides where the uncertainty comes from.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Find one probability estimate you have made or heard in the past week. Ask: which part of the uncertainty would narrow with more information, and which part would remain regardless? Write the estimate as a range with the two components labeled. Notice whether the range changes what action you would recommend.

chapter_evidence.title: Supernewsjunkies?
chapter_evidence.hook: Updating is not a virtue by itself. Any change in an estimate can be called an update. The question is whether the move was the right size for the signal that triggered it. Move too little and the old evidence holds more weight than it deserves. Move too much and you hand the new signal more power than it has earned.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: What distinguishes careful forecasters from those consuming the same headlines and reaching less accurate estimates? The gap is not volume of consumption. It is the ratio of diagnostic content extracted to narrative noise discarded, and that ratio improves with practice, not with more subscriptions. A vivid, detail-rich report can produce worse estimates than a single sentence of clean diagnostic data, because the detail activates the illusion of evidence without adding predictive weight.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Update quality matters more than frequency. Strip the narrative from the signal and move the estimate by exactly what the diagnostic content has earned, no more and no less.
chapter_evidence.try: The next time you read a report or article, count how many sentences contain new diagnostic information versus contextual detail and repetition. Identify the one or two diagnostic sentences. Ask how much your estimate would move if those sentences were verified. Write the number. That is your proportionate update, not the emotional salience of the whole document.
extracts: Tim Minto's forecasting log looked like a gentle staircase: many small steps rather than the cliffs and plateaus that mark a forecaster who holds and then panics.
When a signal was small, the move was small.
Everything else is context.
examples: Ryan moves from 45% to 51% acquittal probability after a strong but impeachable witness statement
Nina holds the broader contamination estimate at 42% after a single new cluster and recommends one more day of sampling
Anders strips the dilution effect from a 12-page shipping report and hedges half the position at 73%
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Before sizing any update, identify the specific evidence that warrants the move and calculate how much that evidence, adjusted for its credibility and base rates, actually changes the estimate. Move by that amount rather than by the emotional salience of how the information arrived.
chapter_evidence.challenge: The next time you receive a detailed report or message, count the sentences that contain genuinely new diagnostic information versus the sentences that provide context, repetition, or framing. Write both counts. Then ask: if you had received only the diagnostic sentences, what would your update have been? Compare that to what you actually felt after reading the full document.

chapter_evidence.title: Perpetual Beta
chapter_evidence.hook: Keeping a forecast record is not the same as keeping an auditable forecast record. A note that reads 'expected the project to go well' cannot be reviewed honestly after it does not go well. The question is whether, at the moment of prediction, you committed to a claim specific enough for the outcome to prove you right or wrong.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The willingness to learn from errors guarantees nothing when memory has already softened the original prediction before the review begins. By the time the outcome arrives, most forecasters' recollection of their own certainty has drifted toward what actually happened. What looks like learning from a mistake is often learning from a revised memory of the mistake. The three requirements for real improvement are a record precise enough to audit, active feedback-seeking rather than passive reception, and a memory discipline strong enough to resist rewriting the past in the light of what happened.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Perpetual beta needs three things: a record precise enough to audit, active feedback-seeking before outcomes arrive, and deliberate resistance to hindsight rewriting. Any one missing makes the other two useless.
chapter_evidence.try: Find one prediction you made in the last month: a project outcome, a client behavior, a conversation you anticipated. Write down exactly what you predicted, as precisely as you can remember stating it at the time. Then write how the outcome compared. If your memory of what you predicted has already shifted toward what happened, you have already experienced hindsight bias. From now on, write predictions at the moment of making them: date, specific claim, specific probability.
extracts: Three things make perpetual beta work as a discipline rather than as a stance.
The imprecise record feels like accountability.
It is rigor about evidence: the record shows what actually happened, the error shows where the model was wrong, and the correction happens before the next similar question, not after.
examples: Sam's engine review flags move 14 as the real error while his two-day replay had blamed move 27
Anke's six-month notebook traces the croissant failures to proofing time, not butter temperature
Aleksy finds an undocumented protocol change behind the patient's three-week plateau
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Write predictions at the moment of making them: date, specific claim, specific probability. When the outcome is known, review the record before forming an explanation of what happened. The explanation must be grounded in what the record shows, not in what makes sense in retrospect.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Write down one prediction you make today before it resolves: a meeting outcome, a client response, a project milestone. State the specific claim and your confidence level. Set a reminder to review the record when the outcome arrives. Do not form an explanation before opening the record.

chapter_evidence.title: Superteams
chapter_evidence.hook: More people working on a forecast does not automatically produce a better forecast. It depends on whether the disagreement among those people is still alive at the moment it could change the estimate, or whether the social pressure to converge has already done its work.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A team's collective estimate is not improved by adding people who share the same view. It is improved by preserving views that diverge until the estimate has been formed. The value of a dissenting voice depends entirely on when it is heard: a reservation voiced before the group settles is a forecasting asset; the same reservation voiced after consensus costs more and helps less.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A superteam keeps disagreement operationally available at the moment it could change the collective estimate. The structural fix is simple: aggregate independently before discussion, not after.
chapter_evidence.try: Before your next team discussion on a forecast or decision, run a one-minute silent estimate round: each person writes a number before anyone speaks. Collect them before opening discussion. Note whether the range is wider or narrower than you expected. If the range collapses to near-consensus after you speak first, your opening framing was already shaping the group's estimates, not wisdom emerging.
extracts: The silent estimate round is a structural intervention, not a trust exercise.
When the aggregation happens first, the range of private estimates is visible before any estimate has been influenced by the others.
That is a different conversation, and it produces different decisions.
examples: Tom flags a contraindicated medication before the attending's protocol begins, reversing the preliminary diagnosis in twelve minutes
Juliette's load-path calculation surfaces two weeks late, pausing a planning submission the partner had already approved
Chidi names a drainage risk at the trail fork; rescuers reach the hiker in the rockfall shelter forty minutes later
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Before any group forecast discussion, collect individual estimates in writing before opening discussion. Voice reservations at the earliest point they can be articulated rather than at the point where they feel fully certain. Treat a dissenting view as a contribution to the collective estimate, not as a challenge to the authority framing the question.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In your next group meeting, try running the silent estimate round before discussion begins: have each person write their estimate on paper before the first person speaks. Collect the estimates and read the range aloud before discussing. Note whether the range surprises anyone. The surprise is information about how much individual variation existed before the group's social dynamics compressed it.

chapter_evidence.title: The Leader's Dilemma
chapter_evidence.hook: Moltke did not give his commanders a script. He gave them a mission, a set of constraints, and the authority to decide everything else as conditions changed. The insight was not about trust in subordinates. It was about information: a battlefield changes faster than any headquarters can process and redistribute. A leader who tries to control every adjustment from the center is not exercising careful oversight. They are creating structural latency at exactly the moment the situation demands speed.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A leader who projects decisive certainty while privately maintaining open questions is not performing strength. They are choosing a pose that makes the organization harder to correct. The precise mechanism is structural: when the leader cannot be seen to doubt, the people closer to the changing conditions have no channel through which to surface what the original plan missed. The organization's ability to revise while action is unfolding depends on whether doubt is an acceptable input to the system, not on how the leader feels about being wrong.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Leadership is a design problem. Mission clarity, explicit constraints, and a reporting condition let local actors exercise judgment without the leader staying close to every decision point.
chapter_evidence.try: For one ongoing project or initiative you lead, write down: the objective in one sentence, the two or three constraints that bound how it can be achieved, and the single reporting condition that would trigger you stepping back in. If you cannot write those three things in under five minutes, you have not yet defined the mission clearly enough to delegate, and your team is probably waiting for approval on decisions they should be making themselves.
extracts: The doer-thinker tension runs through every organization at scale.
A local actor with a clear objective and explicit constraints can exercise judgment.
They are substituting less information for more, which is the structural definition of noise.
examples: Matthew steps back from a ventilator reallocation the ward lead has already made and lets her call stand
Adaeze hands the foreman a written decision rule; the foreman makes a sequencing call that saves four hours on day seven
Olivier issues a three-element sector brief; one sector boss's early resource call lets the command post adjust before the overrun
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Before delegating any initiative, write the mission objective, the constraints that bound it, and the reporting condition that triggers re-engagement. These three elements are the structure that makes decentralized judgment possible without losing the feedback loop that allows correction.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next 24 hours, find one decision you have been approving for a team member that falls within their area of expertise and within your stated constraints. Write the mission objective, the constraints, and the reporting condition, then hand the decision back to them with those three elements written down. Note whether you feel the urge to add clarifying guidance beyond the three elements. That urge is the overcontrol signal.

chapter_evidence.title: Are They Really So Super?
chapter_evidence.hook: Accepting what forecasting cannot do is the beginning of a more precise claim about what it can. Kahneman and Taleb are right that some high-impact events break the frame a forecaster builds to understand them: the rare, correlated, structurally unusual event falls outside the historical base rates that calibration depends on. Accepting that limit does not erase what forecasting can still do. Most decisions live on terrain where careful reasoning, disciplined updating, and honest probability estimates still outperform either overconfident prediction or resigned uncertainty. The skill is sorting the terrain accurately and then doing something useful in both zones.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The most valuable forecasting move for genuinely unknowable probabilities is to stop trying to estimate the probability and ask instead what preparation the possibility demands. An analyst who says 'I cannot give you a reliable number for this tail event' and then proposes a conditional scenario analysis is delivering more useful information than one who supplies a probability that looks precise and is not. The limit, named honestly, redirects effort from a fabricated estimate toward something the decision-maker can actually use.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Kahneman and Taleb's critiques narrow the honest scope of forecasting without erasing it. Where probability fails, the skill shifts: name the limit, then ask what preparation is warranted regardless.
chapter_evidence.try: Find one risk or uncertain outcome in your work or life that you have been trying to put a probability on and cannot, because there are too few comparable historical cases. Instead of forcing a number, ask a conditional question: if this outcome happened, what would you do? What would you need to have in place? Write the conditional preparation steps. Those steps are what forecasting delivers when the probability is genuinely unknowable.
extracts: The argument Kahneman and Nassim Taleb make does not require choosing between trusting forecasting and distrusting it.
The answer requires no probability estimate.
It is the forecaster doing the same work at a different angle.
examples: Jack names what the catastrophe model cannot estimate and recommends a separate tail reserve to the underwriting committee
Margaux refuses a fabricated probability and proposes two conditional scenarios the planning committee can build against instead
Rafael reframes a 3-to-5 percent probability question as a conditional cost comparison and gets the failsafe approved in one meeting
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Sort the questions you face into two categories: those where historical base rates are sufficient to calibrate a reliable estimate, and those where they are not. In the first category, forecast carefully and update. In the second, name the limit explicitly and shift to the conditional question: if this occurred, what should be in place?
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next 24 hours, find one planning document or risk assessment with a probability column containing numbers you do not trust. Pick the highest-consequence item and run the conditional question: if this occurred, what would you do and what would you need to have in place? Write the conditional preparation steps. Note how much more specific and actionable the outputs are compared to the probability number you started with.

chapter_evidence.title: What's Next?
chapter_evidence.hook: Ernest Amory Codman tracked his own surgical failures and presented them in public. His hospital found this less comfortable than prestige, and showed him the door. The system he built, following patients for years and recording complications, failures, and their causes, became the foundation of modern surgical outcome auditing. The lesson his career teaches is not about surgery. It is about what happens to accountability systems when accuracy and institutional comfort are in conflict: the institution wins in the short term, and the accountability system wins in the long run only if someone insists on keeping score anyway.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Scorekeeping makes the gap between persuasive and accurate forecasting visible. Without it, the gap is invisible, and institutions reliably default to rewarding the forecaster who sounds most useful rather than the one who turns out to be most right. A scorekeeping system is therefore both the technical improvement mechanism and the institutional threat: it threatens every reputation built on persuasiveness that has never been checked against outcomes.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Scorekeeping converts a forecast into evidence. Without it, accuracy and persuasiveness are indistinguishable, and institutions reward whichever sounds better. A testable question is as important as a careful answer.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one prediction that you or your organization will make publicly in the next six months, a project completion, a sales forecast, a policy outcome. Break it into three component sub-questions, each with its own trackable indicator and checkpoint date. Write these three sub-questions down. These are what accountable forecasting looks like: not the headline number, but the component questions that let you tell the difference between 'we were wrong' and 'the world changed under us.'
extracts: The superforecaster solves half the problem.
It is a position.
Not a sudden embrace of scorekeeping, but a persistent insistence on keeping score anyway, in public, with specificity, until the accumulated evidence is too large to dismiss.
examples: Luke implements 12-month employment retention tracking; the first cohort returns 61%, not 75%, and she redesigns a program component
Hanna discovers a 71% accuracy rate hidden in a private spreadsheet and proposes the departmental forecast log her colleagues resist
Pablo breaks a single annual revenue forecast into five component questions; the board can finally diagnose rather than just observe the miss
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Before making any significant forecast or commitment, ask three questions: Is this question specific enough to score? If I am wrong, will I know what went wrong? Have I broken this into component sub-questions with their own checkpoints? If the answer to any of these is no, reframe the question before making the forecast.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next 24 hours, find one prediction or forecast your organization has made publicly in the past year that has not been reviewed against its outcome. Score it: was it right, was it wrong, and how confident were you when you made it? If you cannot score it because it is too vague, that is itself a finding: write down what would have made it scoreable, and use that specification for the next forecast you make.

chapter_evidence.title: A Portrait of the Author as a Learning Junkie
chapter_evidence.hook: The first hour looks impossible when you make it carry the price tag of 10,000.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The finish line feels like the honest target. In fact, it can stall the first useful threshold that lets practice begin.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Start by defining the first useful competence line, not the fantasy of mastery, so the awkward opening hours have a job they can actually finish.
chapter_evidence.try: Write one postponed skill, then finish this sentence: I would be usefully competent when I can ____ without help.
extracts: Aanya looks at six basil cells under a clear plastic lid and feels the old ambition trying to swell.
If the answer sounds like a résumé line, it is probably too big.
A clear threshold is also a kindness to the next attempt.
examples: Lukas Stops Pricing Bookkeeping Like Accounting
Camille Tests the Welcome Before Adding Signs
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Define the first useful line before you practice. The skill is not lowering ambition forever, but giving the opening hours a target they can actually reach and test.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one postponed skill and write a one-sentence competence line that starts with: I can use this when I can. Make the line visible and testable.

chapter_evidence.title: 10 Principles of Rapid Skill Acquisition
chapter_evidence.hook: A scuffed radio, a stopwatch, and five bad handoffs can teach faster than a perfect plan.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Effort feels like the accelerator, but actually speed comes from shrinking the loop until each attempt returns a correction.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Rapid progress comes from designing a practice loop where the right subskill is easy to start, quick to correct, and repeated enough to stabilize.
chapter_evidence.try: Draw four boxes for one skill. Label them target / subskill / barrier / feedback. Fill each box before your next practice session.
extracts: Hugo stands beside a bent repair stand tray while a rear wheel ticks through every gear.
Where is your loop still too wide?
Then feed it reps.
examples: Mikkel Clears the Bench for One Grid
Grace Cuts Intake to Three Questions
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Build a practice loop before asking for more effort. The loop should make the right rep easy to start, quick to check, and narrow enough that the next attempt improves.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one skill and write four labels on one line: target, first subskill, biggest barrier, fastest feedback source. Do one rep only after all four are named.

chapter_evidence.title: 10 Principles of Effective Learning
chapter_evidence.hook: Cold mist on a recorder teaches more when Laura predicts the bird before she checks the file.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Preparation feels responsible. In fact, it earns its keep only when it changes the next attempt.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Effective learning turns study into contact: a prediction, scaffold, practitioner cue, or test that makes the next rep clearer than the last one.
chapter_evidence.try: Before your next practice block, write one prediction about what will go wrong and one test that will tell you whether you were right.
extracts: Laura clips a field recorder to a fence post before dawn and hears two calls she keeps confusing.
Laura's prediction changed what she heard at dawn.
Learning earns its place when practice can feel the difference.
examples: Etienne Lets the Checklist Catch the Nut Warning
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Make preparation accountable to practice. Every reading session, model, hook, checklist, or expert cue should change what you try next or how you judge the attempt.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before your next practice block, write one prediction about what will go wrong and one test that will tell you whether you were right.

chapter_evidence.title: Yoga
chapter_evidence.hook: Chalk on a rented shoe can show the same lesson as a yoga mat: remove the fake difficulty first.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Despite looking more serious, the harder version can hide the lesson. Simplify the setting until the instructor can reach the one movement that is failing.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Embodied practice improves when you remove false difficulty, clear the misconception, and let live correction reach one basic movement at a time.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one physical skill, cross out one difficulty that is mostly costume, then write the correction you need on the next basic rep.
extracts: Marco sits on the rowing machine with the performance monitor covered.
The body cannot correct a performance of effort.
It can correct a movement.
examples: Claire Lets One Quiet Foot Teach
Anna Stops Performing the Violin Posture
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Simplify embodied practice until the real movement is visible. Keep the correction channel open, remove the extra performance layer, and repeat the basic rep without pretending the standard got easier.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one physical skill and cross out one difficulty that is mostly costume. Name the one correction you need on the next basic rep.

chapter_evidence.title: Programming
chapter_evidence.hook: Orange expiry stickers beside a copied sheet make programming smaller than the word sounds.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Abstract confidence looks like progress; the real test arrives when code can run and fail in public.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A technical skill becomes learnable when you break it into one runnable slice, run it on a real problem, and let the first error guide the next fix.
chapter_evidence.try: Write the smallest technical output your project could produce today, plus the first thing that might fail when you run it.
extracts: At 8:05 a.m., Paula looks at the laminated feeding chart clipped to one wildlife enclosure.
Concepts still matter.
The closer the error sits to a real form, order, ticket, or claim, the less likely the learner is to turn practice back into theory.
examples: Thomas Runs the Expiry Flag First
David Lets the Comma Break the Parser
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Turn a technical goal into one runnable slice. The aim is to create an output small enough to run today and honest enough to fail in a useful way.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Write the smallest technical output your current learning project could produce today, plus the first thing that could fail when you run it.

chapter_evidence.title: Touch Typing
chapter_evidence.hook: Steno paper beside a covered speed display makes the old shortcut lose its favorite defense.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The old motion is not proof but the rival. Slow the corrected rep until comfort cannot steal the keys back.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Habit repair needs a protected slowdown: repeat the corrected motion through frustration until the old pattern stops winning by feeling easier.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one familiar motion you do poorly, slow one rep below comfort, and name the exact old shortcut you are refusing.
extracts: "Let me move your wrist once," the trainer says as steam fog beads on the stainless pitcher lip.
It is loyalty to the corrected motion at the moment the old one offers escape.
A repaired habit is built by refusing false fluency one visible rep at a time.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Protect corrected repetition from the old pattern's comfort. The work is to slow the rep, name the shortcut, and count only the motions you want to keep.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one familiar motion you do poorly, slow one rep below comfort, and name the exact old shortcut you are refusing.

chapter_evidence.title: Go
chapter_evidence.hook: Colored magnets around two isolation rooms can teach the first Go lesson: read the local fight.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The large board feels like the real skill, but the useful entry is smaller: read one local pressure instead of freezing before the whole map.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Strategic complexity becomes approachable when you stop waiting for total mastery and read one local pattern with one live pressure.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one complex situation and mark the smallest local fight: what pattern repeats, what is under attack, and what must be defended first?
extracts: At 3:37 p.m., Manon stands near muddy cones knocked sideways by the left touchline.
Find the local fight.
Stay humble about the rest.
examples: Jack Defends Payroll Before Chasing the Queue
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Enter strategic complexity through one local fight. Read a recurring pattern, name the active pressure, and choose what to defend or attack without pretending the full board is solved.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one complex situation and mark the smallest local fight: what pattern repeats, what is under attack, and what must be defended first?

chapter_evidence.title: Ukulele
chapter_evidence.hook: Silver harmonica on a toast card asks the real performance question: will this hold for one listener?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The small public slice is not softer but stricter, because a narrow piece must survive real ears before the learner earns more.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Deliberate narrowing works when the small performance subset is rehearsed in isolation and then tested by real ears.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one performance skill and write the smallest piece you would be willing to show one real listener after focused repetition.
extracts: Chris folds six numbered French sentences beside a metro ticket and stops calling the goal conversation.
Public testing is not a finish line.
Do less, but make the less audible.
examples: Olivia Plays Eight Bars for the Best Man
Marta Lets the Camera Catch the Thumb
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Build a public-ready subset. Choose one small piece, isolate the movement that fails, repeat it, and test it with a real listener before expanding.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one performance skill and write the smallest piece you would be willing to show one real listener after focused repetition.

chapter_evidence.title: Windsurfing
chapter_evidence.hook: Green water near a buoy line gives practice a harder teacher than another dry explanation.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Shelter feels safer, but too much shelter lies. The useful answer is not full chaos but a small live slice where the real condition can push back safely.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Condition-shaped skills improve when you isolate one live subskill, repeat it under bounded pressure, and reconnect it to the real environment.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one condition-shaped skill and define the smallest live subskill that could face a real but low-risk version of the environment.
extracts: Catarina used to practice every camera setting at once before outdoor family sessions.
Keep it real.
Let the world push back just enough to teach.
examples: Jonas Tests Edge Recovery at the Current Line
Ryan Keeps the Loaded Turn on the Low Slope
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Design a live but bounded practice slice. Identify the condition that changes the task, isolate one subskill, and test it under a low-risk version of that condition.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Name one condition-shaped skill and define the smallest live subskill that could face a real but low-risk version of the environment.
