chapter_evidence.title: How Can Great Firms Fail? Insights from the Hard Disk Drive Industry
chapter_evidence.hook: The firm that failed had just posted its best quarterly numbers, and every decision that led there was sound.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Failure looks like negligence from the outside. Inside, it looks like a very good quarter. In fact, the same discipline that sharpens execution in an established market can narrow what that market is allowed to show you.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Your current customers define what your business should improve next. That same definition quietly excludes the buyers outside their world, which is where the next market is forming.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one type of buyer who never shows up in your customer feedback. Write down what they use instead of your product. That gap is where the next relevant signal lives.
extracts: Think about what a disciplined customer listening process actually produces.
Then ask which buyers are not.
It requires only that the decisions stay inside the frame the current customers define.
examples: Charlotte Uses Advertiser Feedback to Shelve the Digital Column
James Takes the Franchise Scores to the Investment Committee
David's Survey Finds No Threat from Digital Cameras
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to separate what your current customer feedback can measure from what it cannot, and to treat that gap as a real signal rather than an absence of data.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Name one buyer type that has no voice in your most recent product or investment decision. Write one sentence about what that buyer would say about your product if asked today.

chapter_evidence.title: Value Networks and the Impetus to Innovate
chapter_evidence.hook: The product that failed your quality review this morning may be exactly what someone else's market has been waiting for.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: When you evaluate a new product against your current standards and reject it, even though the rejection is correct for your market, you may be wrong about another one. The quality test you trust is calibrated to the network you already serve.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A value network defines what your organization considers worth building. A product that fails inside one network may be exactly right inside another.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one product or service you recently rejected for not meeting your standards. Write one sentence about what a customer in a different market would find useful about it at exactly this level of quality.
extracts: Consider what an evaluation against current standards actually does.
The checklist was correct.
That is the gap worth closing.
examples: Claire's Benchmark Table Has No Row for Hobbyists
Thomas Runs Restaurant Economics on a Home-Baker Kit
Etienne Declines the App That the Small Shops Already Use
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to separate which evaluation criteria are specific to your current value network from which are universal, and to apply that distinction before using a rejection to close a file.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Name one product or technology your organization rejected in the last year. Write down the three criteria that drove the rejection. Then write one sentence about which of those criteria would not apply if a different type of customer used the product.

chapter_evidence.title: Disruptive Technological Change in the Mechanical Excavator Industry
chapter_evidence.hook: You do not need to win the mainstream on day one. You need one market where your weaknesses are tolerable.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A new product that loses to the established leader on every mainstream measure can still be the right move. In fact, winning in the first market requires only that your advantages are real there and your weaknesses do not matter yet.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A disruptive product needs a first market where its weaknesses are tolerable and its advantages are real, then a path toward the mainstream.
chapter_evidence.try: Name the one use case where your product or idea is already the obvious choice. That is your foothold. Write it down before asking whether it can scale.
extracts: Consider what it takes to find the right first market.
Owning a new technology is not the same as finding the right first market.
The right first market is still invisible.
examples: Rachel's Cargo Bike Fails the Freight Evaluation and Wins the Alley
Andrew Notices His Team Is Using the Wrong Tool for the Right Reason
Lars Evaluates a Route the Major Carrier Left Behind
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to identify the first market where your product's specific advantages are the ones that matter, rather than testing it against the mainstream's full requirement set.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Name one product or initiative that failed your organization's performance evaluation. Write down the one use case where the evaluation criteria would not apply and the product's actual advantages would be the relevant ones.

chapter_evidence.title: What Goes Up, Can't Go Down
chapter_evidence.hook: Every market your organization quietly exits becomes the first step of someone else's climb.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Abandoning a low-margin segment looks like smart financial discipline. It is in fact the moment you hand an entrant their starting position. Unattractive to the incumbent does not mean unimportant to the industry.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Low-end markets too thin for an incumbent's cost structure can be exactly right for an entrant's. Climbing upmarket creates the gap the entrant fills, one segment at a time.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one customer segment your organization has stopped actively serving because the margins were thin. Write down what kind of operator could serve them profitably at a smaller scale.
extracts: Consider how the upmarket migration actually feels from inside the incumbent.
The question is not whether the segment is profitable for you.
It is a strategic one.
examples: Diana Drops Local Music and Hands Off Its Audience
Matthew's Portfolio Improves and the Economy Tier Opens Up
Nicolas Closes Free Access and Does Not Track Where the Readers Go
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to evaluate market exits not only against your own economics but against the economics of an entrant who might find the same segment viable.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Name one customer segment or product category your organization has stopped actively serving in the last three years. Write one sentence about what kind of operator could serve those customers profitably at a different scale.

chapter_evidence.title: Managing Disruptive Technological Change
chapter_evidence.hook: An evaluation designed for a market that already exists will reliably fail to find value in a market that is still forming.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Despite the care applied to evaluating a disruptive effort, the problem is rarely insufficient rigor. The benchmark the rigor measures against is wrong. A proof demand built for a mature market asks an early effort to supply a kind of evidence that market formation has not yet produced.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A disruptive effort in a forming market cannot satisfy mature-market proof demands. Rigor still applies, but aimed at evidence the current stage can actually supply.
chapter_evidence.try: Think of one new effort in your organization that has been evaluated and found lacking. Write down the two or three criteria it was judged by. Then write one alternative criterion that would measure learning progress rather than mature-market performance.
extracts: Think back to the last evaluation meeting where a new effort was presented and found lacking.
The first: does this effort pass our standard evaluation?
Treating it as weaker because it does not convert into numbers the standard framework expects is where the rigor stops being useful.
examples: Emily's Scorecard Has Every Mature Criterion Red
Daniel's Procurement Standard Flags the Startup as Pending
Frida's Board Packet Shows Every Approval Criterion Unmet
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to distinguish the question of whether a disruptive effort passes the standard evaluation from the question of whether the standard evaluation is appropriate for the effort's stage, and to redirect rigor toward evidence the market can actually supply.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Think of one new effort in your organization that has been evaluated and found lacking. Write down the two or three criteria it was judged by. Then write one alternative criterion that would measure learning progress rather than mature-market performance.

chapter_evidence.title: Give Responsibility for Disruptive Technologies to Organizations Whose Customers Need Them
chapter_evidence.hook: The team that owns the new initiative serves customers who do not need it. That is not a leadership problem. It is a placement problem.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The instinct is to place a disruptive effort where the relevant technical expertise lives. The problem is that technical expertise and customer pull are rarely in the same place. In fact, placement determines whose urgency governs the effort, and urgency follows customers, not capabilities.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A unit prioritizes what its customers reward. Place a disruptive effort where those customers don't pull for it, and it will always lose. Placement determines which customers generate urgency.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one new initiative in your organization and identify the team that currently owns it. Write down who that team's three most important customers are. Then write one sentence about whether those customers create pull toward or away from the initiative.
extracts: Think about the last time a new initiative at your organization was prioritized in a resource allocation meeting.
Each unit serves a customer base.
If the disruptive effort is not something those customers need, it will be protected by no one.
examples: Laura's Telemedicine Kiosk Waits in the Wrong Corridor
Ryan's P2P Roadmap Looks Exactly Like Corporate Banking Needs
Julien's Brief Arrives Listing Cable Subscribers as the Audience
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to diagnose whether an initiative is placed inside a unit whose customers generate pull toward it, and to distinguish customer-fit placement from technical-fit placement when choosing where a disruptive effort belongs.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Name one new initiative in your organization and identify the team that currently owns it. Write down who that team's three most important customers are. Then write one sentence about whether those customers create pull toward or away from the initiative.

chapter_evidence.title: Match the Size of the Organization to the Size of the Market
chapter_evidence.hook: Your growth threshold is not a property of the market. It is a property of your organization.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The problem with size filters is not that large organizations apply them. They need to apply them. The problem is treating the filter's output as a verdict on the market itself. A $10 million opportunity rejected because it doesn't move the needle is in fact still a $10 million opportunity. Someone with different economics will find it.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Growth thresholds measure fit with your current scale, not the market's absolute viability. A market too small for one organization can be genuinely real for a smaller team.
chapter_evidence.try: Think of one market opportunity your organization has evaluated and passed on because the size was too small. Write down the revenue or impact threshold that ruled it out. Then write one sentence describing what size of organization would find that exact number meaningful.
extracts: What is your organization's growth threshold?
The threshold is real and it functions as a filter.
It is a verdict on the fit between the opportunity and your organization's current size.
examples: Megan's Pipeline Review Flags the IoT Platform at the Bottom
Jack's Distribution Model Shows 4 Percent and the Board Moves On
Antoine's Market Size Chart Puts Veterinary at 2.5 Percent
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to distinguish between 'this market is too small for our organization's economics' and 'this market is too small to be commercially viable,' and to apply size evaluations relative to organizational scale rather than as absolute verdicts on the market.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Think of one market opportunity your organization has evaluated and passed on because the size was too small. Write down the revenue or impact threshold that ruled it out. Then write one sentence describing what size of organization would find that exact number meaningful.

chapter_evidence.title: Discovering New and Emerging Markets
chapter_evidence.hook: Forecasting an emerging market before entering it is asking a model to answer a question only real contact can answer.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Demanding a clean forecast before entering an emerging market feels like sound discipline. In fact, it is a way of requiring that the market explain itself before you can learn anything from it. Emerging markets cannot produce a forecast. That is what makes them emerging. Discovery is what happens between not-knowing and knowing, and it requires contact, not a model.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Emerging markets lack the information forecasts require. The discipline is to enter with clear learning questions and organized contact. Discovery produces information that forecasts cannot.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one market your organization has decided it cannot enter yet because the forecast isn't clear enough. Write down one specific question, not a forecast but a concrete question, that real contact with potential users would let you answer within the next month.
extracts: Think about a market your organization has decided it cannot yet enter because the forecast isn't ready.
It is waiting for contact.
It is just not the kind that produces a clean number before anyone has set foot in the market.
examples: Anna's Review Surfaces Three Patterns Outside the Trial Protocol
Chris's Pilot Data Does Not Match the Learner Model
Lukas Opens the Second-Week Data and Finds Routes That Are Not on the Map
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to treat the first stage of emerging market entry as a learning exercise organized around specific questions, rather than as a forecasting exercise that must be completed before contact can begin.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Name one market your organization has decided it cannot enter yet because the forecast isn't clear enough. Write down one specific question, not a forecast but a concrete question, that real contact with potential users would let you answer within the next month.

chapter_evidence.title: How to Appraise Your Organization's Capabilities and Disabilities
chapter_evidence.hook: What made you good at this work is not the same as what will make you good at that work.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The self-appraisal problem is not whether the organization has strong capabilities. The problem is that those capabilities were built to produce a specific kind of result in a specific context. When the context changes, the capability continues producing what it was designed to produce, which in fact may no longer be the right thing.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Capabilities embed assumptions about what good work looks like. Fit appraisal asks whether the new context shares those assumptions. Strength in one setting can be an obstacle in another.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one organizational routine your team does exceptionally well. Write down the underlying assumption that routine makes about what a good outcome looks like. Then write one sentence about whether a new market you are considering shares that assumption.
extracts: Think of one thing your organization does exceptionally well.
When that routine moves into a new context, the assumption moves with it.
It is an observation about where it was built to work.
examples: Kathryn's Platform Dashboard Shows 22 Percent Utilization
Thomas's Supplement Line Arrives After Competitors Have Set the Price Point
Hugo's Charging Network App Prototype Meets the Dealer Agreement Clause
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to identify the assumptions embedded in your organization's best routines and appraise whether those assumptions match what a new market or task requires.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Name one organizational routine your team does exceptionally well. Write down the underlying assumption that routine makes about what a good outcome looks like. Then write one sentence about whether a new market you are considering shares that assumption.

chapter_evidence.title: Managing the Strategy Development Process
chapter_evidence.hook: Most strategy processes are optimized for executing a plan. Very few are optimized for updating one when the market contradicts it.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: What looks like strategic discipline is often its own obstacle in a disruptive context. A plan written before the market speaks cannot be held at all costs. The discipline is to set direction and build a process that can absorb what real market contact teaches. A strategy that cannot hear what the market is saying is not rigorous. It is fragile.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A strategy process needs a mechanism for absorbing what market contact teaches. Without it, the process executes a plan the evidence is ready to revise.
chapter_evidence.try: Think of the last time your organization received information that contradicted the current plan. Write down whether that information was absorbed into the strategy or filed as an exception. Name one change to your review process that would make the next signal harder to file away.
extracts: Think about the last time your organization received a piece of information that contradicted the current plan.
That mechanism does not remove rigor from the process.
They are the same discipline, applied at different points in the strategy development process.
examples: Beth's Clinical Dashboard Shows Thirty-One Unsolicited Secondary Mentions
Luke's Reorder Spreadsheet Puts the Seasonal Ale in Row One
Mathieu's Booking Report Shows a Demand Corridor That Is Not on the Network Map
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to identify when incoming evidence is being filed as an exception and to build a review mechanism that evaluates whether that evidence should trigger a strategy revision.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Think of the last time your organization received information that contradicted the current plan. Write down whether that information was absorbed into the strategy or filed as an exception. Name one change to your review process that would make the next signal harder to file away.

chapter_evidence.title: The Dilemmas of Innovation: A Summary
chapter_evidence.hook: Strong firms fail at disruption not because of bad management. The pressures that produce failure are interdependent, and solving any one of them leaves the rest in place.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Understanding each dilemma individually does not give you a way to resolve them as a system. The dilemmas interact: addressing one without the others redistributes the problem rather than eliminating it. Disruption is hard for strong incumbents not despite their strengths but because of them.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Disruption failures are not single-cause. The pressures (customer dependence, value network, capability mismatch, size mismatch, strategy rigidity) interact and compound. The lesson is a diagnostic map, not a checklist.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one challenge your organization is treating as a single-lever problem. Write down two other pressures that are connected to it. Then write one sentence about what you would need to address all three, and whether that is currently possible.
extracts: There is a version of the incumbent failure story that attributes everything to bad management: the leaders who could not see what was coming, the organizations too slow to adapt, the cultures that resisted change until it was too late.
Their best customers were generating the returns that funded everything.
But seeing it clearly is the beginning of managing it.
examples: Kate's Whiteboard Has Five Circles and No Outward Arrow
Tom's Three-Year Log Shows Twelve Quality Decisions and Zero New-Model Investments
Vincent's Whiteboard Has Four Boxes and No First Move
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to diagnose which combination of interacting disruption pressures is active in your organization's situation, rather than treating any single pressure as the problem to solve.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Name one challenge your organization is treating as a single-lever problem. Write down two other pressures that are connected to it. Then write one sentence about what you would need to address all three, and whether that is currently possible.

chapter_evidence.title: The Habit Loop
chapter_evidence.hook: A man with memory loss turns left at a garden door, and the routine knows what he cannot say.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Why does the same morning route survive job changes, moves, and even new partners? In fact, automatic behavior is readable long before anyone tries to praise it: Soren maps the cue, routine, and reward arc of his own coffee ritual and finds the loop already named.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Automatic behavior becomes usable evidence when you separate the cue, routine, and reward, because a visible loop can be diagnosed before it is judged or changed.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one repeated action from today. Write three evidence labels: what happened just before it, what your body did next, and what changed afterward. Do not fix it yet.
extracts: Eugene Pauly stands at the edge of a familiar route with no clear story for why he is moving.
It is diagnosis.
A loop you can see is a loop you can work on.
examples: Rina Stops Correcting the Hallway Walk
Ishani Names the Click, Reach, and Quiet
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The skill is loop diagnosis before judgment. You practice pausing long enough to separate the signal, the repeated act, and the payoff. Once the sequence is visible, you can decide whether to support it, interrupt it, or redesign it.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next 24 hours, pick one repeated action you can observe without changing it. Write a three-line loop note with evidence only: cue, routine, reward.

chapter_evidence.title: The Craving Brain
chapter_evidence.hook: The banana peel is still in her hand, but the rent-credit tally has already made sorting feel worth it.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A reminder only points; it does not pull. The stronger move is to make the cue carry a near, specific payoff, so the reader, climber, student, or customer can feel the reward before the routine has started.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A cue becomes sticky when it starts promising the reward in advance, because anticipation turns a reminder into a pull toward the routine before the first move.
chapter_evidence.try: Put one cue for a wanted routine beside a tiny preview of its payoff: a finished line, saved photo, checked card, or first sound. Notice whether the preview makes you reach sooner.
extracts: A compost poster can be perfectly clear and still lose.
It was the anticipated reward attached to the cue.
A cue that previews the right reward becomes a hand on the shoulder.
examples: Maris Lets Four Clean Bars Play First
Orla Watches the Warm-up Bell Work
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The skill is making the payoff arrive early. You look at a cue and ask whether it merely reminds, or whether it lets the expected reward be felt before the routine starts. Strong cues preview the real payoff, not a random prize.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next 24 hours, choose one wanted routine and add a payoff preview to its cue: a photo, sound, tally, sample line, or finished-state image you will see before starting.

chapter_evidence.title: The Golden Rule of Habit Change
chapter_evidence.hook: The last-call sign goes dark, and the old pour has a new middle before the room goes quiet.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: What looks like a clean break is usually a stalled swap. Attacking the cue or denying the reward backfires; Mireille keeps both outer pieces in view, builds a new routine for the same payoff, and writes a short script for the night stress calls the old path back.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Habit change holds when the cue and payoff stay visible, the routine in the middle changes, and support is ready for the hour pressure returns.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one unwanted routine. Write the old cue on the left and the real reward on the right. Add one new middle action and the person or object that will hold it under pressure.
extracts: A red ticket curls from a jammed printer above the seafood pass, and the old path opens in less than a second.
The same reward is pursued.
The new middle has to be waiting where the old middle used to live.
examples: Zadie Changes the Pour After Last Call
Rui Calls Reset Instead of Snapping
Dima Moves Five Chips After the River
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The skill is building a replacement that answers the same demand as the old routine. You do not start with a nicer action. You start with the cue and payoff, then design a new middle that can survive pressure.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next 24 hours, choose one unwanted routine and build a three-part swap: old cue, same reward, new middle. Add one support person, script, or object to hold it under pressure.

chapter_evidence.title: Keystone Habits, or The Ballad of Paul O'Neill
chapter_evidence.hook: The empty clamp groove is small enough to miss, and strong enough to make four departments tell the truth.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A habit's noble label rarely picks the keystone. The opposite is closer: the routine that earns the name is the boring one that forces cleaner reporting, faster escalation, and visible accountability the rest of the team can use.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A keystone habit matters because its spillover changes the surrounding system: reports, handoffs, accountability, trust, and small wins all start moving.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one team routine and draw four arrows from it: what report changes, what handoff changes, what trust changes, and what mistake becomes visible sooner.
extracts: One instrument tray reaches the operating room with a clamp missing from its slot.
It is not yet a keystone.
It is the one that makes the rest of the room move.
examples: Blythe Points to the Empty Groove
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The skill is tracing spillover before choosing the habit. You look for the routine that forces facts, handoffs, and accountability to move across a system. A keystone habit is selected by the changes it causes around it.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next 24 hours, pick one routine at work or home and draw a four-arrow spillover map: report, handoff, accountability, and small win.

chapter_evidence.title: Starbucks and the Habit of Success
chapter_evidence.hook: The gift receipt hits the counter, and the first sentence arrives before the seasonal bookseller can freeze.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: If self-control depended on raw character, the calmest barista would crack first under a rude customer. Instead, Onyeka rehearses the first line and the apology gesture before the cue arrives, so willpower runs as a practiced script.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Willpower becomes more reliable when the stressful cue has already been paired with a practiced first response, so pressure triggers a script instead of improvisation.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one stressful cue you can predict. Write the first sentence you want available, say it out loud twice, then place the cue word beside it.
extracts: A delay board shows two hours beside a quiet MRI hallway.
Stay calm is not a first line.
Rehearsal gives pressure a road to follow.
examples: Maelle Practices With the Bent Gift Receipt
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The skill is rehearsing the first response before pressure arrives. You name the stressful cue, write the opening move, and practice it out loud in a close version of the real scene. The goal is not to remove stress, but to give stress a trained path.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next 24 hours, pick one stressful cue you can predict. Write the first sentence, say it aloud twice, and put the cue word beside it where you will see it.

chapter_evidence.title: The Power of a Crisis
chapter_evidence.hook: The thawed inventory sheet is still wet when the lab director changes who must answer the next alarm.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Despite the smoke and the search for who owns the failure, the lasting payoff of a crisis is structural. Cordis, the new ops lead, uses the exposed gap to wire a fresh reporting routine before fear fades and the old shortcuts harden again.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A crisis changes an institution only when a leader converts the exposed breakdown into a specific new routine for reporting, escalation, or accountability before old habits return.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one recent group breakdown. Write the old routine it exposed, then choose the single handoff, signoff, or escalation step that should exist before comfort returns.
extracts: A warm milk crate sweats on a pantry loading dock after a holiday closure.
A new habit has to catch the work before the old one closes around it.
If you use it only for apology, blame, or inspiration, the old habit waits.
examples: Sabela Adds the Second Alarm Signature
Veyra Tapes the Alert Card to the Console
Eamon Gives Every Trade a Stop-Work Tag
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The skill is turning a breakdown into a redesigned routine while the old one is still visible. Name the failed institutional habit, then install one concrete reporting, handoff, escalation, or accountability step at the point of failure. Move before embarrassment fades and the organization explains the accident away.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next 24 hours, choose one recent group breakdown. Write the sentence: "The old routine was..." Then add one new handoff, signoff, or escalation step that should be in place before the next similar moment.

chapter_evidence.title: How Target Knows What You Want Before You Do
chapter_evidence.hook: The broth, crackers, and Tuesday pickup slot do not know the diagnosis, but they know enough to tempt the store.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Habit trails reveal less than they seem to and more than the seller admits. In fact, Lior, the retention designer, reads them as partial prediction first, then tests whether each nudge helps the customer or quietly steers a tired choice.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Habit trails become powerful when organizations read them from the outside, but every use has to pass the test of whether it serves the person or merely steers them.
chapter_evidence.try: Open one recent trail you leave: receipts, logins, routes, or skips. Circle a repeat, then write one helpful use of that pattern and one manipulative use.
extracts: Single-serving soup cards replace family-size dinners in a meal-kit menu queue.
Habit data has power because it sees repeated action before the person may have named the change.
Then design as if the person on the other side deserves both help and room.
examples: Nessa Chooses the Familiar Coupon Strip
Bram Places Winterization Beside the Paint Trays
Cyra Points at the Sleep-Timer Button
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The skill is reading repeated external behavior without pretending it tells the whole story. Notice the trail, state the inference as partial, and then test the use: does it help the person, or does it steer them when they are exposed, tired, or uncertain?
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next 24 hours, pick one trail you leave outside yourself: purchases, app opens, route choices, skips, or reorders. Write one helpful use, one manipulative use, and the design line between them.

chapter_evidence.title: Saddleback Church and the Montgomery Bus Boycott
chapter_evidence.hook: The elevator sticker curls by the mailboxes, and the first two signatures make silence harder to keep.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Quiet agreement reads like support even though it moves no one. The hidden engine is a visible, repeated role: Bashir takes the first shift among close friends, then the same task spreads through weaker ties and peer expectation.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Movements spread when private agreement becomes visible participation, first through strong ties, then across weak ties, and finally through repeated group expectations.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one cause people around you quietly support. Write one close-tie starter, one weak-tie bridge, and one weekly visible act people could repeat.
extracts: A stall map is smudged with rain near a stack of folding tables.
The role can be small.
That is how a cause moves from what people quietly support to what they expect each other to do.
examples: Imani Starts the Mailbox Repair Ledger
Nolwen Pins the First Heat Card
Cassia Stamps the Cleared Market Path
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The skill is turning private support into a visible participation routine. Start with close ties who will act first, build a bridge for weaker ties to see and copy, and make the act repeat on a schedule. Do not count agreement as action until people have a role they can keep in public.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next 24 hours, choose one cause people near you privately support. Write one strong-tie starter, one weak-tie bridge, and one visible weekly act with a place, time, and role.

chapter_evidence.title: The Neurology of Free Will
chapter_evidence.hook: The sleep-clinic note lies beside the hotel key, and the old mystery now has a door wedge.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A weak habit explanation begs for blanket pardon even though the strong form names the moment the loop became foreseeable. Devika asks that question first, then contains, redesigns, or avoids the cue before the next exposure repeats the harm.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Automatic routines complicate responsibility, but once a risky loop is known and foreseeable, accountability returns as a duty to contain, redesign, or avoid it.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one loop that could hurt someone if repeated. Write the cue, the likely harm, and the containment you would put in place before that cue appears again.
extracts: An orange hold flag sits beside a month-end invoice queue.
Responsibility returns before the next cue.
It has to be visible enough that doing nothing becomes a choice.
examples: Kiran Asks for the Door Wedge
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The skill is moving from explanation to accountable redesign. Name the cue, name the likely harm, and decide whether the right response is containment, changed conditions, or avoiding the cue. The test is whether the next exposure is safer, not whether the person sounds more aware.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next 24 hours, choose one loop that could harm someone if repeated. Write the cue, the harm, and one containment that will be in place before the cue appears again.

chapter_evidence.title: Introduction
chapter_evidence.hook: The room has three doors, each one marked with a cost somebody real will have to carry.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The mistaken move is to hunt for a clean framework after the clean options are gone. Instead, name the cost of each path and keep responsibility for the call.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: The struggle is not a failure of leadership. It is the operating condition where partial information, real costs, and responsibility meet in one decision.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one live decision with no painless option. Write the concrete harm caused by each path, then circle the harm you are willing to own before asking for more analysis.
extracts: At 5:12 p.m., the legal note lands in the CEO's inbox while the sales team is still celebrating a contract in the next room.
Which promise would be broken in public?
You make a constrained call, you tell the truth about its cost, and you stay close enough to repair what the call damages.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice converting vague pressure into owned tradeoffs. In a hard call, write known facts, unknown facts, harms by option, and the person accountable for execution before you seek emotional relief.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, pick one unresolved work decision with no clean answer and draft a four-line tradeoff note: known fact, unknown fact, harm of option A, harm of option B.

chapter_evidence.title: From Communist to Venture Capitalist
chapter_evidence.hook: A past can sharpen your eye and still bend your aim when the room has changed.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The mistaken move is to treat formation as automatic credibility. Instead, ask which old reflex helps the present facts and which one has become bias.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Origin stories are useful evidence, not verdicts. They explain how a leader reads authority and incentives, but present conditions still have to test the reflex.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one strong instinct you use at work. Write where it was learned, then write one current condition that could make that instinct mislead you.
extracts: The hiring committee loves the candidate's story before it has tested the job.
It may be strength.
Use them to see how the driver learned to steer, then look through the windshield before deciding where the road goes now.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use formation as a diagnostic lens. When a strong instinct appears, ask where it was learned, what it helped solve, and whether today's incentives, authority, and scale still match that old world.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, choose one instinct you trust at work and write three lines: where you learned it, when it helped, and one current condition that could make it wrong.

chapter_evidence.title: I Will Survive
chapter_evidence.hook: The old scoreboard still glows, but the only number that matters now is how many moves remain.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The mistaken move is to prove commitment by clinging to the old growth plan. Instead, reset success to the next interval of cash, trust, and execution.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: When the market invalidates the old plan, survival means buying the next real decision with truthful communication, cash control, execution, and reassessment.
chapter_evidence.try: For one pressured project, replace the normal success metric with the next survival interval: cash, time, trust, or capacity needed to reach one more disciplined decision.
extracts: At 9:05 p.m., the financing email arrives with terms that would have sounded insulting six months earlier.
Maybe the answer is cash.
The goal is to still have a company capable of making a better constrained call when the next facts arrive.
examples: Emily Names the Missing Tour Dates
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice replacing invalidated success metrics with survival intervals. Define the unit that buys another decision, communicate the frame, execute inside it, and reassess before the frame expires.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, choose one pressured project and write its survival interval in one measurable unit: days, dollars, capacity slots, delivery cycles, or trust-critical accounts.

chapter_evidence.title: This Time with Feeling
chapter_evidence.hook: The second alarm sounds while your hands are still dirty from the first one.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The mistaken move is to trust experience automatically after a prior save. Instead, add decision hygiene because memory and fatigue can distort the next call.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Recurring strain needs a visible decision structure so experience can inform the call without letting fatigue, memory, or numbness quietly choose for you.
chapter_evidence.try: Before your next repeated hard call, write four words on the page: tradeoff, owner, consequence, review. Fill one concrete sentence under each before acting.
extracts: After the first outage, the operations chief acted fast and got praised for it.
Write tradeoff, owner, consequence, review.
Decision hygiene keeps the room awake.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Build a small decision hygiene habit for repeated pressure. Before acting, identify the current tradeoff, the owner, the consequence of being wrong, and the review signal that will force a new look.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, find one repeated work problem and fill four one-sentence fields for it: tradeoff, owner, consequence, review signal.

chapter_evidence.title: When Things Fall Apart
chapter_evidence.hook: The rumor has already found the hallway; leadership has to catch up with facts.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The mistaken move is to confuse toughness with blunt speed. Instead, use clear candor, dignified people calls, and controlled execution before delay multiplies harm.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: When collapse starts, private pressure has to become shared facts, clean ownership, dignified people decisions, and execution that refuses rescue fantasies.
chapter_evidence.try: Find one fact people are likely to learn through rumor. Write the exact plain sentence that states it, the affected group, and the next decision boundary.
extracts: At 8:10 a.m., the operations chief sees two versions of the company forming.
Who is affected?
The product is a shared map and a controlled next move.
examples: Julia Posts the Lost Contract Number
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Convert private pressure into usable facts and clean execution. State the fact plainly, name affected people, assign ownership, reject unconfirmed rescue plans, and protect dignity through sequence.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, identify one fact your team may learn through rumor and write the exact sentence, affected group, owner, and next decision boundary.

chapter_evidence.title: Take Care of the People, the Products, and the Profits, In That Order
chapter_evidence.hook: The profit leak starts on the floor where two supervisors teach the same job differently.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The mistaken move is to chase margin or morale as separate problems. Instead, inspect the people system producing product misses before profit is treated alone.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: People systems create product reliability, and reliable products create durable profit. Weak training and unclear standards become financial problems later.
chapter_evidence.try: Take one recurring product or financial miss and name the manager behavior, training gap, or unclear standard that could be producing it upstream.
extracts: At the bakery, the owner wants to blame flour because flour feels easier to replace than management habits.
A strong people system has visible artifacts.
Treat the people system as a production system, and the product and profit numbers start making more sense.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice tracing weak output upstream before reacting to the financial symptom. Look for management debt in training, standards, role clarity, feedback, incentives, and accountability.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, choose one recurring miss and trace it to one likely upstream management gap: training, standard, owner, feedback, or incentive.

chapter_evidence.title: Concerning the Going Concern
chapter_evidence.hook: The founder's open door becomes a traffic jam once twelve teams need the same answer.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The mistaken move is to add process because headcount grew. Instead, replace personal access with mission-linked ownership, cadence, and escalation rules.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A going concern needs operating architecture: clear owners, useful cadence, escalation paths, stage-fit leaders, and behavior loops that carry the mission.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one recurring escalation that still depends on personal access. Write the owner, cadence, and exception rule that would let the organization handle it without you.
extracts: At a small company, the founder's judgment can cover a surprising amount of missing structure.
Executive fit changes too.
Ownership, cadence, escalation, and culture loops are how distance stops becoming drift.
examples: Beth Moves Staffing Out of the Hallway
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice designing around recurring decisions, not around abstract size. For each escalation, define the owner, cadence, exception threshold, and behavior loop that keeps the mission visible.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, pick one decision that still reaches you by personal access and write its owner, cadence, exception rule, and first review date.

chapter_evidence.title: How to Lead Even When You Don't Know Where You Are Going
chapter_evidence.hook: The team does not need your certainty; it needs the next step to survive contact with the unknown.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The mistaken move is to perform confidence when answers are incomplete. Instead, use bounded clarity: what is known, what remains unknown, and who owns the next move.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Under ambiguity, leadership is accurate direction: name the knowns, bound the unknowns, assign the next move, and keep behavior consistent with the message.
chapter_evidence.try: Write a three-line update for one uncertain situation: what is known, what is not known yet, and the next move with owner and time boundary.
extracts: The ferry board blinks delayed, and every captain reads the port manager's shoulders before reading the memo.
She wants to wait because the next fact might make the message cleaner.
Lead with the part of the map you actually have, then assign the next step on purpose.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice accurate direction under ambiguity. Separate evidence from inference, write a bounded update, assign one owner, and make your behavior match the message until the review time.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, write a three-line update for one uncertain situation: known fact, unresolved question, next move with owner and review time.

chapter_evidence.title: First Rule of Entrepreneurship: There Are No Rules
chapter_evidence.hook: The policy in your hand may be protecting yesterday's risk while today's risk walks past it.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The mistaken move is to treat no rules as permission to wing it. Instead, preserve the principle while testing whether the rule still fits timing, leverage, and consequence.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: No rules does not mean no standards. It means judgment must test each rule against context, timing, leverage, trust, and the tradeoff in front of you.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one rule you are about to enforce. Write the principle it protects, the current fact that may change its fit, and the boundary that would make an exception legitimate.
extracts: At the hangar, the no-cannibalization rule looks absolute until a rare parts shortage grounds aircraft that could otherwise fly safely.
Principle: what risk or value does the rule protect?
It is discipline without autopilot.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice reading rules instead of obeying or breaking them reflexively. Name the principle, test present context, define any boundary, assign ownership, and mark the return path.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, choose one rule you plan to enforce and write three lines: principle protected, fact that could change fit, and legitimate exception boundary.

chapter_evidence.title: The End of the Beginning
chapter_evidence.hook: The signature is dry, but the habits that saved the company are still walking the halls.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The mistaken move is to let a good outcome explain every painful tactic. Instead, audit what cost too much, what principle travels, and what must end.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Closure is not the same as interpretation. A transition should separate the result from the costs, preserve durable principles, and retire temporary tactics.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one completed hard period. Draw three columns for outcome, cost, and principle to carry, then put one item in each without letting the outcome explain the rest.
extracts: The most dangerous story after a hard period is the neat one.
Leaders may keep tight control because tight control once prevented collapse.
It is the first moment when leaders can choose which parts of the struggle become wisdom and which parts are finally allowed to stop.
examples: Marianne Keeps the Principle, Not the Panic
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice interpreting success without flattening the hard period. Separate result, cost, durable principle, temporary tactic, and the leadership identity needed for the next stage.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, choose one completed hard period and fill four lines: outcome, cost, principle to carry, tactic to retire.
