chapter_evidence.title: Being Wrong Less
chapter_evidence.hook: Packing tape on Maire's sleeve catches before the missing receipt catches her eye.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: What looks like decisiveness is often just an untested assumption getting expensive. Better judgment starts when the first possible error is still small enough to bruise.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Cut avoidable mistakes by rebuilding claims from what you actually know, testing the weakest assumption early, and keeping the first cost of being wrong small.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one live decision and write the sentence, "This fails if I am wrong about ___." Fill the blank, then choose one cheap test you can run before the next commitment.
extracts: Soraya sets six dead radios in a row at 11:05 at night and writes one sentence on the drill report: assumed batteries held charge.
You do not need to make every choice small forever.
Confidence that has survived a test is different from confidence that has only survived a meeting.
examples: Maire stops the crate over one missing receipt
Kwame asks what the mud did not explain
Janel watches the compliment list stay blank
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The core skill is reducing self-created mistakes before they become expensive. Rebuild claims from facts, name the fragile assumption, and design a first test small enough to teach.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within the next 24 hours, pick one decision you are leaning toward and write the weakest assumption on paper. Before you commit, send one email, run one trial, or check one record that could prove that assumption wrong.

chapter_evidence.title: Anything That Can Go Wrong, Will
chapter_evidence.hook: A split trash bag behind the bike shed tells Ivo his neat new rule has already learned to backfire.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A clean rule can become a dirty instruction once rewards touch it. The real test is not what the plan says, but what shortcut it makes rational.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Judge a rule by the behavior it will create under pressure, then design guardrails for incentives, workarounds, and delayed costs before the rule goes live.
chapter_evidence.try: Before changing one rule, write the behavior it will reward, the shortcut it may invite, and the future cost it could hide. Fix the worst failure path first.
extracts: Marisol stands by press line three at 5:55 in the morning with orange lockout tags spread across the table.
If nobody can say how the rule might be gamed, the room has not finished thinking.
It works because it has already made room for human response.
examples: Galen pauses before writing closed tickets
Fariha counts cough drops beside perfect attendance
Ivo hears the bag fee leak downstairs
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The core skill is reading a rule as a system, not a sentence. Look for incentives, workarounds, spillover, and delayed costs before you trust the first visible improvement.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within the next 24 hours, choose one rule, metric, or habit you rely on. Write the behavior it rewards, the easiest workaround, and one delayed cost, then adjust the rule to reduce the worst failure path.

chapter_evidence.title: Spend Your Time Wisely
chapter_evidence.hook: A wet pipette rack at 6:04 a.m. is where Odelia's future month is quietly being made.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The real cost is not the hour you spend; it is the stronger future you displace. A full week can still be a bad investment.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Spend time well by protecting the few repetitions that build future capacity, naming the best alternative you are giving up, and designing around present bias.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one repeating action worth protecting this week. Put it on the calendar first, then write the best thing it will displace so the cost is visible.
extracts: Veda stands beside a laundry basket at 10:44 at night with a glowing charging cable in her hand.
She has to write the lost practice under each option before the tradeoff becomes real.
Shape the room so your tired self can follow the plan your clearer self chose.
examples: Odelia signs the wet calibration log
Reuben finds the course hidden under good yeses
Kiko hears tomorrow morning in the locker room
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The core skill is selecting and protecting high-return repetitions. Treat every recurring yes as a tradeoff, then design the environment so present comfort does not keep raiding the future.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, pick one compounding routine and give it the first protected slot on tomorrow's calendar. Then write the less important activity it will replace so the tradeoff is explicit.

chapter_evidence.title: Becoming One with Nature
chapter_evidence.hook: Lemon-soap jugs under a hand-lettered sign can show whether effort fits the system or fights it.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: What looks like weak effort is often a system before fit, momentum, or threshold. Push harder only after you know which force is missing.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Read the system before forcing effort. Check fit and flywheel cost first, then use thresholds and reinforcing loops to decide when to persist, adjust, or stop.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one stalled effort and write three checks: what the environment rewards, what would make the next push easier, and what threshold would change the pattern.
extracts: A barcode scanner chirps at the east-branch help desk at 1:37 in the afternoon while Hafsa watches the first twelve people join a shared hold-alert group.
What would make the next push easier?
It rewards patterns that can survive in the environment they actually meet.
examples: Corin moves the refill jugs into the flow
Zuleika traces the overnight win back six weeks
Ansel hears what the garden selected for
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The core skill is reading change as system behavior. Diagnose fit, startup effort, threshold effects, and reinforcing loops before deciding whether to push harder or redesign.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, choose one slow effort and identify whether the problem is fit, startup drag, a missing threshold, or no reinforcing loop. Make one small design change tied to that diagnosis.

chapter_evidence.title: Lies, Damned Lies, and Statistics
chapter_evidence.hook: A cracked phone screen can make one scary story feel larger than the rate it came from.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The real test is not whether a number sounds precise; it is whether the base rate and comparison frame arrive before the number gets authority.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Before reacting to a vivid number or story, find the base rate and denominator first. Add the comparison group so evidence has scale instead of just force.
chapter_evidence.try: Take one number you saw today and write its missing comparison: compared with what group, what time period, and what usual rate?
extracts: Quillan sits at a diner counter at 7:05 in the morning with cold toast beside his notebook and a police scanner murmuring near the pie case.
The base rate is that anchor.
A rate tells you how far the warning should travel.
examples: Esma waits before moving the roadmap tile
Dax checks the quiz against the old stack
Rocio lets her aunt ask the rate question
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The core skill is giving numbers context before they guide action. Anchor vivid stories and sharp percentages with base rates, denominators, and comparison groups.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, find one headline, dashboard number, or family-chat claim and add the missing frame: usual rate, raw count, denominator, and comparison group.

chapter_evidence.title: Decisions, Decisions
chapter_evidence.hook: Color-coded magnets on a staffing board can turn one awful feeling into three visible paths.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: One heavy mood can smuggle several futures into the same room. A decision tree does not remove uncertainty, but it makes each path answer separately.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Improve hard choices by splitting the decision into options, branches, consequences, and unknowns, then compare the paths instead of trusting one global feeling.
chapter_evidence.try: Take one decision you keep describing as stressful. Draw three options, then write the main consequence and unknown under each one.
extracts: Hester leans over a laminated marsh map at 4:03 in the morning while her headlamp cuts a white circle through the dark.
Do not worship the tree.
A visible choice is not an easy choice, but it is finally a choice you can inspect.
examples: Leandra splits the unsafe weekend into branches
Sacha stops calling both paths scary
Nuri unbundles the lease she already signed
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The core skill is decomposing a hard choice until its paths can be compared. A good decision tree makes options, consequences, and unknowns visible without pretending uncertainty disappeared.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, draw a decision tree for one live choice. Include at least three options or branches, one consequence under each, and one unknown you can investigate this week.

chapter_evidence.title: Dealing With Conflict
chapter_evidence.hook: Punch cards scattered under a time clock can show when another correction only feeds the contest.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The real move is not to win the sentence but to choose the reply the sentence will invite. In conflict, a truer point can still make the wrong game stronger.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Handle conflict by reading the interaction as a system: notice incentives, legitimacy, and the larger outcome before deciding whether to press, reframe, concede, or walk away.
chapter_evidence.try: Before your next hard reply, write what the other person is likely to do after hearing it. If your move rewards the wrong response, choose a different move.
extracts: Oskar holds a stapled plant newsletter at 5:44 in the morning while copies still feel warm from the break-room machine.
She is choosing the level of conflict that matters.
Then choose the move that changes the conflict, not the one that only proves you can swing harder.
examples: Yasuko stops before the second public correction
Raffi sees why the same complaint needed another carrier
Helmi names the late guests under the dishes
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: The core skill is reading conflict as an interactive system. Before responding, inspect the likely next move, the authority structure, the visible battlefield, and the larger outcome.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within 24 hours, choose one live or recent conflict and map the loop: your move, their likely reply, the incentive it creates, and the larger outcome you want to protect.

chapter_evidence.title: Effectiveness Can Be Learned
chapter_evidence.hook: Your report is almost polished. What if the polish is hiding work no one can use?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Despite Harry S. Truman's plain public style as U.S. president, effectiveness did not rest on charm. It rested on habits that pushed decisions into useful results.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Effectiveness is learned when you ask who will use your work, aim time at that result, and practice the habits until pressure arrives.
chapter_evidence.try: During your next conversation about your week, ask one person, "Which meeting should I shorten or drop?" Say their exact answer back, then make that calendar edit.
extracts: Laura has a full lobby, a donor update, and a payment file that keeps sliding to the bottom of the pile.
You already know how to work hard.
It is training yourself to know when the useful result is clear, and when your busy work is hiding from it.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice asking who will use your work before you polish it. The skill is to move from private proof to outside contribution, then place time where the result will actually be used.
chapter_evidence.challenge: During your next conversation about a result someone needs from you, say: "Before I polish this, what will you use it to decide?" Then move one calendar block toward that answer.

chapter_evidence.title: Know Thy Time
chapter_evidence.hook: 4 steps; only 1 exposes the lie. The calendar cleanup comes after the record.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A full calendar can look like proof that time is under control. In fact, it often hides a memory problem in neat boxes.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Know your time before you defend your calendar: record what happens, cut what should not exist, and protect blocks for work that needs judgment.
chapter_evidence.try: After your first coffee, move one sticky note onto your keyboard with this boundary: "I can help after I see what this removes."
extracts: Clifford's hospital administration corridor makes the softer version of this idea feel thin.
If a patient need is new, answer it.
Then remove what should not happen again.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice making a time record before you accept your own story about the week. The skill is simple: write what actually happened, ask what should disappear, then protect blocks for work that needs judgment. Use the boundary, "I can help after I see what this removes," when pressure tries to turn every request into your problem.
chapter_evidence.challenge: For your next workday, move one notebook beside your keyboard before opening messages. Record requests as they arrive and write one boundary when a request has no clear contribution.

chapter_evidence.title: What Can I Contribute?
chapter_evidence.hook: A Sears, Roebuck and Co. retailing slip moves toward a shelf no shopper can use.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Why does good work still miss? Because contribution is judged by the result someone else can use, not by how hard the work felt inside the job.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Ask what contribution the situation needs, then shape your work around direct results, values, and people development that others can actually use.
chapter_evidence.try: Within the next 24 hours, when input is requested, count activity-first replies. Record one handoff note: "They need ___ from me."
extracts: Jade's unanswered volunteer message sits on her phone while the American Red Cross roster looks full.
Without that result, contribution talk becomes self-display.
With the precondition in place, the question gets bracing: who needs this, what can they do with it, what standard does it set, and who becomes more able because it exists?
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice naming the result before naming the activity. Ask what direct result, value, or people development the situation needs. Then shape your output so another person can use it without guessing.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a request lands on your desk or phone, observe and count whether your first response names activity or contribution. Record one tally and one handoff note.

chapter_evidence.title: Making Strength Productive
chapter_evidence.hook: 4 strength sources sit on the table; the visible flaw is rarely where the work begins.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Strength is not a kindness badge, but a work design claim. If Warren cannot name what the person does well, he is only hiding from the staffing decision.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Build work around usable strength, then guard against weakness where it can break trust, fit, or results; absence of flaw is not the same as performance.
chapter_evidence.try: Before you send your next reply, put FIT? on a sticky note, ask one person what strength they need from you, then write one line from their answer.
extracts: Robert E.
Then clear more room for that work.
Fit is the test before any assignment.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use the Strength Fit Note before you assign work or answer a request. Write one line that names the strength the work needs and the person who can supply it. Then add one guardrail for any weakness that could affect trust, fit, or results.
chapter_evidence.challenge: For the next 24 hours, put FIT? on a surface you see often. Before you answer one work request, write one line naming the strength the request truly needs.

chapter_evidence.title: First Things First
chapter_evidence.hook: Could the request you want to answer be the one that tells you what must stop?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Useful work can become the enemy: when every good task keeps its claim, the few great tasks never get enough attention.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Put first things first by naming what stops, what waits, and what gets enough attention to finish.
chapter_evidence.try: The next time you feel pulled toward the newest request, place your priority note by the keyboard and draft: "I can take this if we stop ___."
extracts: The cost shows up before the benefit.
Drucker is not asking you to become careless.
The gain is that your best attention finally reaches the work that can repay it.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Name the Stop by pairing every priority with the work that will stop, wait, or lose resources. The skill keeps concentration honest. You are not choosing first things until a lower-value claim has actually been deprived.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within the next day, pre-write one reply for the moment a new request crowds your priority: "I can consider this if we stop or delay ___." Move that draft beside the artifact you check most.

chapter_evidence.title: The Elements of Decision-making
chapter_evidence.hook: 2 of the 5 decision elements start after agreement, where many bad choices quietly fail.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: What looks like delay is actually speed insurance. A decision gets faster when you first name the kind of problem, the result it must meet, and the person who will act.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Decide by running the elements in order: classify the problem, name the must-meet result, choose the right answer, assign action, and check reality.
chapter_evidence.try: At your next handoff, touch your laptop lid and add one tick beside the choice if it names the owner, date, and first feedback check.
extracts: A clean decision memo can still leave dirty work behind.
A decision without an owner still has not left the room.
Use them when the cost of a wrong assumption would be paid by everyone after the meeting.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use the Decision Tick Check before a choice leaves your hands. Make one visible mark only when the decision names the problem type, the must-meet result, the owner, the date, and the first feedback check.
chapter_evidence.challenge: For 24 hours, attach the Decision Tick Check to the laptop lid you already close between tasks. At each handoff, record one tick only when owner, date, and feedback are named.

chapter_evidence.title: Effective Decisions
chapter_evidence.hook: The approval memo leaves the room before anyone writes the second option.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A fast yes can look brave and still hide the real choice. Real speed comes after the alternatives are visible.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Effective decisions need real alternatives and named evidence before commitment. They also need an owner who turns the chosen path into checked action.
chapter_evidence.try: Before your next decision meeting, ask one person, "What view am I rushing past?" Write the answer and rehearse pausing quick agreement once.
extracts: A wall of agreement feels good when the room is tired.
When action is needed, dissent has to stay disciplined.
The dissent belongs in drills and reviews, not in the instant when seconds decide harm.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice making one hidden default visible before you commit. Name the main option, force one real alternative, and ask what evidence would test both. Then assign the action so the decision leaves the room.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before you start your next decision conversation, stage the first minute once. Say the two alternatives, name the evidence test, and pause the habit of accepting quick agreement.

chapter_evidence.title: Investment versus Speculation: Results to Be Expected by the Intelligent Investor
chapter_evidence.hook: Liam watches a buy button glow on his banking dashboard, then pauses when the famous name still fails the investment test.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A respectable label can still hide speculation. The operation earns the word investment only when analysis, principal protection, and adequate return are all present.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Before you buy, fill in three blanks: analysis, principal protection, and adequate return. If one is blank, keep the move out of investment money.
chapter_evidence.try: Open one holding you are tempted to buy or keep, and mark whether analysis, principal protection, and adequate return are all present.
extracts: The investment/speculation split is a practical test for a purchase before money leaves the account.
Risk appetite without analysis is speculation.
If any answer is blank, the purchase has crossed into speculation.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use a short audit before treating any security purchase as investment. The skill is to require analysis, principal protection, and adequate return together, then match the effort level to defensive or enterprising behavior instead of using risk appetite as proof of discipline.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before the next purchase or keep decision, run the same audit on one candidate: analysis, principal protection, adequate return, and whether the effort matches defensive or enterprising behavior.

chapter_evidence.title: The Investor and Inflation
chapter_evidence.hook: Getting every dollar back can still leave you poorer when inflation has cut what those dollars buy.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Fixed-dollar claims can look intact while purchasing power erodes, and familiar hedges can fail at the wrong price or structure.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Judge every inflation hedge by purchasing power after price, structure, and taxes, not by nominal repayment or a label that sounds protective.
chapter_evidence.try: Add a recurring calendar trigger named Inflation check. When it opens, mark any fixed-dollar holding, common stock position, or bond position that you are treating as automatically protected from inflation.
extracts: Inflation changes the unit of judgment.
The point is not that stocks are useless against inflation; it is that price and valuation still matter.
Inflation protection is strongest when a claim survives all three lenses instead of looking attractive under only the first.
examples: Delaney Checks The Bond's Real Cost
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use a calendar trigger to separate nominal safety from purchasing-power safety before you accept a default choice. The checklist is simple: fixed-dollar claims can repay principal while losing purchasing power, stocks can fail as an automatic inflation hedge, and bonds can carry inflation risk even when credit risk is low.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Create the calendar trigger and run it once on one fixed-dollar claim, one common stock position, or one bond position. Write pass only when you can name the inflation risk you checked.

chapter_evidence.title: A Century of Stock-Market History: The Level of Stock Prices in Early 1972
chapter_evidence.hook: Sarah sees a high early-1972 market level in a note and almost treats the price alone as the verdict. Then she asks what earnings, dividends, and bond yields say together.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A high market level can warn you, but it cannot judge itself. Price needs earnings, dividends, and bond yields in the same frame.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Judge a market level by what the price buys: earnings, dividends, and bond yields together matter more than the headline price alone.
chapter_evidence.try: Send one message before the next market-level decision: "Can we put price beside earnings, dividend yield, and bond yield before treating this as attractive or expensive?"
extracts: The useful question is not whether the market looks high in isolation.
Ask what earnings sit under that price.
The discipline is simpler and more useful: connect any story about the future to the price paid, the earnings behind it, the dividends received, and the bond yield available elsewhere.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Before accepting any market-level claim, ask for the price level beside earnings, dividend yield, and bond yield. Treat the answer as a combined expected-return check, not a verdict from one attractive metric.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one market-level claim already on your list. In one message, request the matching price, earnings, dividend yield, and bond yield, then leave the decision open until all four are visible together.

chapter_evidence.title: General Portfolio Policy: The Defensive Investor
chapter_evidence.hook: Lana hears a confident market forecast and checks whether her policy would let one opinion move the whole portfolio.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The boring boundary is the active tool: it stops a defensive investor from turning a forecast into an all-or-nothing bet.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Set the defensive mix before the market tests you: stocks and bonds may move inside the band, but the band keeps one forecast from becoming the whole portfolio.
chapter_evidence.try: Write your current stock and bond percentages, mark the 25 percent and 75 percent boundaries, and circle any sleeve that would break the policy after one proposed trade.
extracts: The defensive policy begins with a boundary, not a forecast.
If bonds offer a better fit for the person, the bond sleeve can rise.
The next action is already visible: check the band, check the quality, check the tax result, and make the smallest adjustment that restores the plan.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Set the defensive mix before the market tests you: stocks and bonds may move inside the band, but the band keeps one forecast from becoming the whole portfolio. The practice is to compare every proposed trade with the 25 to 75 percent boundary before money moves.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Write your current stock and bond percentages, mark the 25 percent and 75 percent boundaries, and circle any sleeve that would break the policy after one proposed trade.

chapter_evidence.title: The Defensive Investor and Common Stocks
chapter_evidence.hook: Peyton wants safety, but the safer move is not avoiding every stock; it is buying common stocks only through repeatable standards.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Defensive stock ownership is not excitement in disguise. It is a controlled program with quality, price, dividend, and diversification checks.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A defensive stock program is allowed, but only as a rule-bound sleeve: quality, dividend record, diversification, price, and the bond mix all have to fit.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one stock or fund you would be tempted to buy, then write one quality reason, one price limit, and how the purchase would change the stock-bond mix.
extracts: Defensive stock ownership is permission with conditions.
The stock sleeve must also fit the bond sleeve.
That small delay is the defensive investor acting with discipline, not retreating from common stocks altogether.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: A defensive stock program is allowed, but only as a rule-bound sleeve: quality, dividend record, diversification, price, and the bond mix all have to fit. The practice is to make the purchase wait until the stock passes those tests and still belongs inside the total portfolio.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one stock or fund you would be tempted to buy, then write one quality reason, one price limit, and how the purchase would change the stock-bond mix.

chapter_evidence.title: Portfolio Policy for the Enterprising Investor: Negative Approach
chapter_evidence.hook: Milo sees a high yield and treats refusal as laziness until the credit risk shows what the extra income is asking him to ignore.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The enterprising investor does more work, but the first useful work is negative: knowing which offers should be refused.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: For the enterprising investor, avoidance is work: reject categories where yield, novelty, or complexity asks you to accept risk you cannot appraise.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one tempting high-yield or new-issue offer, write the extra income or story in one line, then write the credit, legal, political, or incentive risk beside it.
extracts: The enterprising investor needs a negative policy because activity creates temptation.
It is policy.
When that proof is missing, passing is the disciplined result.
examples: Adeline Adds The Country Risk Line
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: For the enterprising investor, avoidance is work: reject categories where yield, novelty, or complexity asks you to accept risk you cannot appraise. The practice is to name the credit, currency, legal, or incentive risk before the offer is allowed onto the research list.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one tempting high-yield or new-issue offer, write the extra income or story in one line, then write the credit, legal, political, or incentive risk beside it.

chapter_evidence.title: Portfolio Policy for the Enterprising Investor: The Positive Side
chapter_evidence.hook: Hugo moves a rejected idea back onto his price-review block, then pauses when the note asks whether disappointment lowered price while real resources remain.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The active move looks like buying what everyone admires. The useful move demands a measurable discount before acting.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Enterprising work begins when price, appraisal, records, and a clear value path all support the same active decision.
chapter_evidence.try: Make one receipt line before keeping an active idea: depressed price with resources, NCAV from current assets minus all liabilities, or price materially below conservative appraisal.
extracts: Enterprising investing has a positive side, but it is narrower than the word active makes it sound.
A bargain is not a low price but a tested discount.
The question is whether the receipt shows price below a conservative view of value.
examples: Hugo Starts With The Unpopular Candidate
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Treat every active idea as unfinished until it has a value receipt. The receipt must show why price is below a conservative view of value: disappointment with resources still present, a severe NCAV floor, or a material gap below conservative appraisal. End each active review with a receipt that names price, appraisal, resources, and the specific value path.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one active idea and write its receipt in plain text. Mark which test it uses: large unpopular company with resources remaining, NCAV from current assets minus all liabilities, or price materially below conservative appraisal. Leave it pending if the receipt is blank.

chapter_evidence.title: The Investor and Market Fluctuations
chapter_evidence.hook: One bad quote can feel like a judgment, but a quote deserves power only after it is tested against your own value note.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The useful response to market noise is not speed. It is the right to buy, sell, or ignore an offer while value stays separate from price.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Treat each quote as an offer: compare it with value, check the asset mix, and choose buy, sell, or ignore only when the appraisal supports the move.
chapter_evidence.try: Open one decision log row for the next quote that pressures you, and fill four cells: quote as offer, value note, asset-mix check, and buy, sell, or ignore.
extracts: The core move is to separate an offer from an appraisal.
The investor may also ignore the quote.
The intelligent act is to let the market serve you with offers while your value work decides which offers deserve a response.
examples: Jordan Treats The Quote As An Offer
The Margin Repair After a Famous-Company Shortcut
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use a decision log to turn each market quote back into an offer. The skill is to write the independent value note before acting, then decide whether the offer belongs in the buy, sell, or ignore column. Practice by logging the quote, value note, and chosen response before any trade caused by a market swing.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before the next market-driven trade, complete one decision-log row with the quote, value note, asset-mix check, and the chosen response.

chapter_evidence.title: Investing in Investment Funds
chapter_evidence.hook: What changes when Brigitte's shortlist sorts by last year's winner first? In her fund-choice note, the bright ranking becomes a warning that a style cycle may already be turning.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The easy move is to chase the fund with the best recent record. The sounder move asks whether the ranking came from a fading style cycle, then checks costs, loads, structure, process, and policy fit.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Start by treating a recent fund winner as a question, not a shortcut. Costs, structure, process, diversification value, and policy fit decide whether it belongs.
chapter_evidence.try: Edit one fund shortlist so no candidate can stay marked ready unless it has separate lines for recent performance, costs, and fund structure.
extracts: A fund should earn a job before it earns a dollar.
Fund type also has to match policy.
The aim is to use them as tools, with each fund tied to a clear portfolio role and tested before recent popularity gets a vote.
examples: A Chat Rebuilds The Price Check
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Change the buying environment so a fund cannot ride on reputation alone. Treat recent performance as a lead, record the cost drag before net return, and flag closed-end structure when share price can differ from net asset value. Keep each fund on probation until ranking, cost, and wrapper price have each earned a written line.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before the next fund decision, add three required fields to the shortlist: why recent performance is not the whole case, what fees or loads reduce return, and whether structure can separate share price from net asset value.

chapter_evidence.title: The Investor and His Advisers
chapter_evidence.hook: An adviser can move an allocation worksheet forward, but the loss still lands in your account unless the advice is tested before it is followed.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The misleading default is to treat hired help as transferred judgment. The sounder move keeps ownership of the decision and checks incentives, role, records, promises, authority, and fit.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Keep judgment with the owner. Use advice for help. Check pay and role, verify records, limit authority, and match promises to the right benchmark.
chapter_evidence.try: Open one adviser proposal or blank worksheet and add a two-minute audit row: loss stays with owner, fee structure, and broker/adviser role.
extracts: Adviser selection starts with a hard ownership fact.
The question is whether the advice is prudent enough to follow.
The aim is to use help without surrendering judgment.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Treat outside advice as a proposal to audit, not a transfer of responsibility. The audit checks who still bears the loss, how commissions, asset-based fees, or hourly fees may shape the recommendation, and whether the person is selling securities or giving ongoing fiduciary advice. Practice by marking every adviser proposal with owner responsibility, fee structure, and broker-or-adviser role before accepting it.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before the next adviser conversation, fill one audit row with responsibility, fee structure, role, and the missing due-diligence items: registration, disciplinary history, scope, custody, and benchmark.

chapter_evidence.title: Security Analysis for the Lay Investor: General Approach
chapter_evidence.hook: At the bond quote sheet, the high coupon looks generous until coverage asks whether the issuer can keep paying.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The obvious move is to reach for the higher yield. The safer move checks interest coverage first, because a fat coupon is worth little when payment strength is thin.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Start with payment strength and normalized earning power. Then let conservative growth, assets, debt, dividends, multiples, and market context decide what price deserves trust.
chapter_evidence.try: During the next weekly calendar review, add a note for a bond or stock idea and fill these checks: interest coverage, normalized earnings power, and conservative growth assumption.
extracts: Begin with the obligation that has to be paid.
The multiple paid for earnings has to be read with care.
When the inputs are estimates, the price paid must leave room for being wrong.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use a weekly calendar review to make valuation wait for the basic checks: a bond needs interest coverage before yield attraction, a stock needs normalized earnings power before the latest profit number, and growth estimates need conservative assumptions. Practice by marking coverage before yield, normalized earnings before latest profit, and conservative growth before a value note is allowed to advance.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before the next review, calculate interest coverage on one bond note, then write a one-sentence verdict: coverage margin adequate, earnings normalization needed, or conservative-growth case too fragile.

chapter_evidence.title: Things to Consider About Per-Share Earnings
chapter_evidence.hook: What if the EPS line in Lane's broker statement is the least useful number on the page?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The misleading default is to treat EPS as a clean answer. It may leave out costs or move them, so the first job is to read the footnotes and ask what changed.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Treat EPS as a claim to test before it guides value. Read footnotes, smooth odd years, judge special charges, check dilution, and compare profit with cash.
chapter_evidence.try: For the next EPS-based idea, send a one-message request: "Please send the footnotes, adjustment list, multi-year earnings, and any special charges; I am keeping the idea pending until those are visible."
extracts: A prospectus packet can make one line feel final.
Profit and cash are not the same signal.
EPS becomes useful after it survives those checks.
examples: When The Latest Year Wins Too Fast
Special Charges Do Not Vanish On Command
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Treat EPS as a claim that needs a source check, not as a finished answer. Before the idea advances, ask for footnotes, adjustment details, multi-year earnings, and special charges so the headline number cannot hide reclassified costs, cyclical distortion, or repeated exceptions. Practice by keeping every EPS-based idea pending until footnotes, adjustments, average earnings context, and special-charge judgment are written in the same saved template.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before the next EPS-based decision, classify one adjustment as recurring or one-time, then compare reported EPS with cash generation before the idea advances.

chapter_evidence.title: A Comparison of Four Listed Companies
chapter_evidence.hook: A comparison sheet lands with four companies at the top, but the useful question sits lower: what price buys what record?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The obvious move is to pick the strongest name. That can fail because recognition is not valuation, and a high price can drain future return.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Compare price with record before reputation leads. Quality and growth still need price, debt, assets, and dividend checks.
chapter_evidence.try: Open one current stock candidate and add a default comparison row: price, earnings, dividends, assets, debt, growth record, and business quality. Leave the buy box blank until the row says whether quality deserves the price and whether growth is already capitalized.
extracts: A side-by-side comparison begins with a modest act.
Growth also needs a price tag.
Compare the record, then ask what the price demands from the future.
examples: Roland's Growth Bet Hits The Rim
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Swap the name-first default for a comparison row before a candidate can stay ready. The row should put price beside record, quality beside valuation caution, and growth beside the question of how much expected growth is already capitalized. Practice the Sunday valuation reset by requiring every candidate to show price, earnings, dividends, assets, debt, growth record, and business quality before it keeps a place on the active list.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before the next day ends, pick one current candidate and complete the default comparison row. Keep it pending if price, record, valuation caution, and growth capitalization cannot all be written down.

chapter_evidence.title: Stock Selection for the Defensive Investor
chapter_evidence.hook: The small stock that feels early can be the first one a defensive screen should keep out.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The misleading default is simple. Small growth feels safer because the story is fresh. A defensive screen asks for size, finances, and records first.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Use the defensive screen to reject doubtful stocks first. Size, finances, stable earnings, dividends, growth, and moderate prices must work together.
chapter_evidence.try: For one stock candidate, write one pass/fail sentence on adequate size, strong financial condition, and earnings stability across years before you look at the valuation.
extracts: The useful stock list is shaped by the names that never enter it.
The aim is not explosive growth.
The cleanest defensive decision may be the stock that never reaches the buy pile.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use the defensive screen as an exclusion device, not a search for exciting exceptions. A candidate stays pending until the record answers the early gates for size, balance-sheet strength, and steadier earnings, then clears the remaining dividend, growth, and valuation checks together. Practice by sending any stock idea with missing size proof, weak financial evidence, unstable earnings, or unfinished dividend, growth, and valuation checks back to the Friday evidence log.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before the next stock decision, create a Friday evidence log row with a ready/pending mark, blanks for size, financial condition, and earnings stability, plus a note for the remaining defensive tests.

chapter_evidence.title: Stock Selection for the Enterprising Investor
chapter_evidence.hook: At a coworking lounge, Violet circles a low P/E list, then pauses before the cheapest name gets to win by default.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Obvious advice says buy the cheapest name. The stronger move starts with the low P/E group, then tests whether the business can support the bargain.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Start with bargain screens. Trust cheapness only when asset cushion, dividends, financial strength, diversification, review, patience, and records all support it.
chapter_evidence.try: Open the next stock idea note and add one gate line: low P/E group, market price versus current assets minus all liabilities, and whether it belongs in a 20-stock bargain group.
extracts: A bargain screen feels clean because it turns messy judgment into rows.
A cheap stock with weak finances may be cheap because debt can stand ahead of the value.
Without the attention to maintain screens, review candidates, and revisit holdings, active methods lose their discipline and drift into speculation.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use a written gate before any enterprising bargain moves forward. First place the idea inside a low P/E group, then compare any net-net claim with market price versus current assets minus all liabilities, and finally confirm it belongs in a 20-stock group so a hidden problem cannot dominate the result. Practice by ending each bargain-stock conversation with the same marks: low P/E group checked, net-net cushion checked, and 20-stock group checked.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before the next stock-selection conversation, sort low P/E candidates into three piles: strong enough for analysis, too weak financially, and too dependent on one apparent bargain.

chapter_evidence.title: Convertible Issues and Warrants
chapter_evidence.hook: At a reception desk, Weston watches a bond offer slide across the counter with a stock option attached. The extra feature can cost more than it gives.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A hybrid label can feel safer than plain stock. The better check splits bond safety from option value before the offer gets credit.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Analyze hybrids twice: test bond safety, then price the option through conversion price, call terms, yield sacrifice, and dilution before accepting the package.
chapter_evidence.try: For one convertible or warrant candidate, write the conversion price or exercise price on the same line as bond safety, income, and expiry risk; reject vague optionality.
extracts: The attractive part of a hybrid issue is also the part that makes it easy to misread.
Then move to the option side.
Only after those pieces stand on their own does the package deserve a place in the decision.
examples: A Counter Receipt Changes Marshall's Answer
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use a receipt check before a convertible or warrant gets a place on the active list. For a convertible, write the bond-side answer apart from the option-side answer, then show the conversion price before giving the option credit. For a warrant, mark no income and possible expiration before the low price can count as safety. Practice by keeping any convertible or warrant note pending until its receipt separates bond safety, conversion price, and warrant income or expiry risk.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before the next hybrid-security review, create a receipt template with blanks for bond side, conversion price, income, and expiration. Use it on a convertible or warrant candidate before it leaves pending.

chapter_evidence.title: Four Extremely Instructive Case Histories
chapter_evidence.hook: In a break room, a familiar railroad name sits on a checklist, and the safest-looking line suddenly needs proof.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Fame can make danger feel settled. Penn Central's 1970 bankruptcy shows why a known name still needs credit work.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Demand plain evidence from every security. Fame, deal growth, financing complexity, promotion, and weak governance can make risk look safe.
chapter_evidence.try: Open a decision-log row for a holding or candidate; fill cells for name safety, acquisition or accounting concern, and financing complexity. Mark it pending if any cell is unclear.
extracts: Case histories can look like dated names, yet they are useful when read as repeated stress tests for evidence.
Promotion can make thin evidence look solid.
Simple proof will not catch every danger, but it blocks the easiest false comfort: the belief that complexity must contain a bargain.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use a decision log to make prominence, acquisition growth, and complex financing earn written evidence before money moves. The log separates name recognition from issuer strength, acquisition excitement from debt and accounting risk, and complicated securities from visible owner economics. Practice by keeping Penn Central, Ling-Temco-Vought, and NVF / Sharon Steel risk prompts in the decision row before approving a holding.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Use the next security review to complete a decision-log row for a holding or candidate: name safety, acquisition or accounting risk, financing complexity, and a pending, reject, or continue mark.

chapter_evidence.title: A Comparison of Eight Pairs of Companies
chapter_evidence.hook: Which claim deserves Carmen's capital when one familiar stock and a second offer compete for the same money?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Judging one company alone can feel complete. A paired check changes the view by making price, risk, and opportunity cost compete.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Compare each valuation with a nearby alternative. Judge price against risk and quality, then test growth and business economics.
chapter_evidence.try: When a favorite stock looks obvious in its own note, add a peer line with the alternate claim, risk difference, and premium evidence.
extracts: A single stock can make its own story feel complete.
Current earnings can sit at a peak or a trough.
Business quality, financial strength, growth, earnings pattern, price premium, and cycle exposure all have to argue with one another before a decision deserves confidence.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Make every candidate compete with a nearby claim on the same capital before it can move forward. Edit the note so the favored name shows its peer, the risk differences that change the comparison, and the quality premium that still has to be earned. Practice by holding each paired valuation note at pending until price, risk structure, and premium evidence appear in the same line.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next candidate note, choose one peer and set the maximum premium the stronger business can justify before the expected return becomes too thin.

chapter_evidence.title: Shareholders and Managements: Dividend Policy
chapter_evidence.hook: Proxy notice in hand, Alice stops reading the stock as only a moving price and starts asking what ownership requires.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Watching price feels practical. Owner thinking asks whether management earns the right to keep profits and whether voting rights, reports, and dividends are being ignored.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Own the claim. Require proof for retained earnings, judge dividends as return, and use voting rights to test capital discipline.
chapter_evidence.try: Run a two-minute owner audit on one holding: write whether profits are kept, what cash is paid out, and what owner right you have ignored.
extracts: The first error is to shrink ownership into a price chart.
Look at earnings retained.
The discipline is plain: follow the money, demand a reason, and remember that ownership includes decisions as well as prices.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use the holding note as an owner audit, not a price-watch log. Mark whether management is keeping profits, write the evidence that keeping them can serve owners, and add cash returned to the return record. Practice by making every shareholder note end with retained profits, cash returned, and the voting or report check you will actually use.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before the next decision on a holding, add an owner-audit row with blanks for profits kept, cash paid out, reinvestment evidence, and any voting or report item you need to review.

chapter_evidence.title: "Margin of Safety" as the Central Concept of Investment
chapter_evidence.hook: Your careful price can still fail when it leaves no room for error, trouble, or a wrong estimate.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Safe-looking names are not enough. Safety comes from price below careful value, so error and trouble have space to land.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Demand a price below conservative value. Use coverage and earning power. Add growth caution, diversification, and temperament to leave room for being wrong.
chapter_evidence.try: Set a calendar trigger to update a saved margin template with conservative value, price, bond coverage when relevant, diversification note, and a pass-or-hold mark.
extracts: Margin of safety starts with a plain test: pay less than a careful value estimate.
Demand value above price.
Then leave the case alone when the gap is too thin.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use a calendar trigger to keep each buy decision tied to a saved margin template. Fill conservative value, the price you would pay, a coverage line for any bond claim, and a diversification note before an idea can move from watch to buy. Practice by letting a candidate advance only when its saved margin entry shows value above price, repayment coverage where relevant, and diversification against single-holding failure.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before the next buy decision, write price, conservative value, coverage, and diversification into one safety sentence; reject the idea when the allowance is absent.

chapter_evidence.title: Man Boobs
chapter_evidence.hook: 1 soft-looking body can become your default, and your forecast pays the bill.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: An expert can know the game and still overweight the body in front of him. The audit asks which cue actually predicts wins.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Trust the scout less when the cue is vivid and the feedback is thin; rank what you can see against what predicts the outcome before you spend a pick.
chapter_evidence.try: Before your next shortlist, place the relevant document beside the page; rank the first visible cue against two outcome signals.
extracts: The Rockets' edge began with a humble question: what if the room is sure for the wrong reason?
That question does not insult the scout.
In daily life, it means asking whether your clearest impression has earned the right to steer the bet.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice catching the cue that grabs your eye first. Name what outcome it claims to predict, then rank it beside two quieter signals. The skill is not doubting everything; it is making the loudest cue earn its weight.
chapter_evidence.challenge: For one day, place the relevant document beside the page before each judgment call. Write the first visible cue and the outcome that would prove it.

chapter_evidence.title: The Outsider
chapter_evidence.hook: I once mistook a crisp uniform for character; Kahneman learned to check the facts underneath.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Despite its haunted start, outsider sensitivity is not a romance about trauma. It is a habit of asking whether the strong impression can predict anything.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Outsider sensitivity means doubting a vivid impression, including your own, until feedback shows whether it predicts the outcome you care about.
chapter_evidence.try: When a recent miss comes up in conversation, spend 10 minutes counting confident explanations before anyone names the result that would test them.
extracts: Separate ratings sound dull beside a young soldier trying to lift a pole over a wall.
A first impression can stay in the room, but it has to stand beside separate marks and later results.
Kahneman's better path was stricter and more useful: delay the grand label, break the judgment into parts, and let results humble the feeling of knowing.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice turning a confident impression into a testable forecast. Check the Forecast by writing what you think you know, naming the outcome it predicts, and looking for feedback before you treat the impression as truth. The skill is not cold doubt; it is a slower path to better judgment.
chapter_evidence.challenge: When someone talks through a recent miss today, count each time a vivid explanation outruns evidence. Mark the first result that could test the story.

chapter_evidence.title: The Insider
chapter_evidence.hook: A live torpedo sits in the dust; do you trust the brave insider or ask what made him useful?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: It is easy to read Tversky as the charming opposite of Kahneman. In fact, his charm mattered because discipline, taste, and math kept it from becoming noise.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Run the Insider Test: when confidence impresses you, look for the ballast beneath it: discipline, problem taste, and the skill to keep moving.
chapter_evidence.try: During your next coffee or commute, write INSIDE on a surface you see. Ask one person, "What made that confidence useful?" Count three details before you answer.
extracts: Barbara Gans keeps the portrait from becoming a rescue poster.
Command of a problem is different.
A loud person can still move the room; they just may move it away from truth.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice checking confidence before you follow it. Run the Insider Test: name the shine, then name the ballast beneath it. Look for discipline, problem taste, and a method that can outlast the person's voice.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Mark INSIDE on a sticky note or page margin you already see. During the next routine conversation, ask one person, "What made that confidence useful?" Count three concrete details before you decide.

chapter_evidence.title: Errors
chapter_evidence.hook: Why did the scolded flight cadet seem cured while the praised one slipped?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Why does experience sometimes teach the wrong lesson? A swing back toward average can look like proof that praise failed or punishment worked.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: When results swing sharply, name the pattern before you praise or blame: regression and sampling noise can make a vivid story feel like proof too soon.
chapter_evidence.try: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a result feels obvious, pre-write two replies: "This may be skill" and "This may be noise." Name the difference.
extracts: Iris can see why the instructors resisted.
Is the result extreme?
It cannot replace direct action when the next minute is the whole case.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice naming the pattern before you name the person. Ask whether the result was extreme, the sample was small, or the forecast was never scored. The skill is not doubt for its own sake. It is a short pause before praise, blame, or confidence hardens.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a result feels obvious, pre-write the actual reply you will use. Compare two explanations in the words: "This may be skill" and "This may be noise."

chapter_evidence.title: The Collision
chapter_evidence.hook: Your first answer arrives wearing a lab coat, and you may never ask who dressed it.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The spark is not a meet-cute, but a method. A sharp clash over probability turned clean models into questions real experts could fail.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: When a tidy model feels too neat, turn the doubt into a testable question. The useful collision is the one that makes judgment visible.
chapter_evidence.try: Before one important response, draft one sentence naming the evidence that would make you change your mind.
extracts: Sawyer pays for the method before the meeting starts.
The old reply would be fast: eight is not enough.
The harder gift is a habit of pausing before the answer hardens.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice turning a neat first answer into one testable question. Use the One-Rehearsal Test: before you reply, say one sentence that names what evidence would change your mind. This keeps doubt practical instead of vague.
chapter_evidence.challenge: For one day, when your fingers reach the keyboard for an important response, draft one sentence: what evidence would make your current answer weaker?

chapter_evidence.title: The Mind's Rules
chapter_evidence.hook: 3 blank answer lines looked neutral, while the first number quietly tugged the pencil.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Useful shortcuts, repeatable mistakes: the same rule that saves work can swap a hard question for an easier one.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Fast judgment gets safer when you ask which rule is working: similarity, easy recall, or a starting number that has pulled the answer toward itself.
chapter_evidence.try: The next time you feel the pull to trust a fast answer, write it once, count 3 cues that made it feel easy, then name the rule steering it.
extracts: Brooke's pencil stops over the letter K.
One checks whether the first number deserves power.
Identify the shortcut, then ask whether the moment deserves the slower answer.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice naming the quick rule before you accept the answer. Ask whether the pull came from similarity, easy recall, or a starting number. The skill is not distrust; it is knowing when a fast answer deserves a guardrail.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next day, stage one fast-judgment moment once: write the fast answer, label the likely rule, and add one check before acting.

chapter_evidence.title: The Rules of Prediction
chapter_evidence.hook: When I trust one vivid case, how far should I move my forecast?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: What looks like bland caution is actually respect for evidence: start with the class, then move only as far as the case earns.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Strong impressions can help prediction, but only after you start with the class, check validity, and pull extreme forecasts toward the average.
chapter_evidence.try: At your next handoff between tasks, place a 3-minute calendar block named Shrink the Forecast. Count six slow breaths, write the base rate, then adjust one prediction.
extracts: Jean's pen hovers over the lower forecast, and the discomfort is not mathematical.
One forecast can be lucky.
Care can be personal; prediction must be checked.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice shrinking a forecast before it hardens. Start with the class, ask how well this kind of evidence predicts, then move only partway from the base rate. The move protects a vivid case from becoming a prophecy. It lets strong evidence count without letting it take over.
chapter_evidence.challenge: During the next 24 hours, use a timer or calendar block at your next transition between tasks. Count six breaths, name one base rate, then shrink one forecast before acting on it.

chapter_evidence.title: Going Viral
chapter_evidence.hook: The hospital chart looked settled, but the missed clue was hiding in the first label.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Expert judgment can save lives and still need a guardrail. The danger is not stupidity; it is a smart person trusting the first clean story too soon.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Kahneman and Tversky's ideas went viral because they helped experts catch predictable errors before a vivid case or early label hardened into judgment.
chapter_evidence.try: Before you start your next judgment call, spend ten minutes writing one line: "The first story pulling me is ___."
extracts: Wallace's counter-case is a patient whose symptoms truly fit the first label.
That boundary matters because the research could be misread as a war on expertise.
It uses it before certainty gets too comfortable.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice catching the first story before it becomes the only story. Write a one-line backup note that names the early label, vivid case, or familiar pattern pulling your judgment. Then ask what evidence would still matter if that first story were wrong.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before one important decision in the next 24 hours, write one line: "The label, case, or pattern pulling me is ___." Then look for one fact it hides.

chapter_evidence.title: Birth of the Warrior
chapter_evidence.hook: When your gut grabs the vivid story first, who checks it before the room moves?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Despite the romance of the warrior-scientist, the lesson is colder: fear makes old stories feel like facts.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Under stress, do not worship confidence. Run a pressure check: name the vivid story, find the missing fact, and slow the first answer.
chapter_evidence.try: During your next conversation about a rushed decision, count three facts the group can see, then say: "Before we move this time slot, which story are we trusting?"
extracts: A decorated memory can help or harm, depending on how the room uses it.
Name the story that feels obvious.
Judgment under stress begins there: not with less courage, but with courage aimed at the first answer.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice catching the story that feels most obvious when pressure rises. Run the Pressure Story Check by naming the vivid cue, naming the story built from it, and asking for one fact that could weaken the story. The skill does not block action; it keeps action tied to evidence.
chapter_evidence.challenge: During one pressured conversation today, say one sentence aloud: "The story I am trusting is __, and the fact that could weaken it is __." Fill both blanks before the choice hardens.

chapter_evidence.title: The Isolation Effect
chapter_evidence.hook: Your marked-up page looks careful, but the hidden frame is doing the choosing.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The easy assumption is that a cautious person will stay cautious. In fact, the same person may guard a gain and gamble inside a loss.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Risk taste changes when the frame changes: before trusting a sure gain or a bold gamble, first name the reference point and compare the common parts.
chapter_evidence.try: During tomorrow's first coffee at your usual seat, move the next request note beside your cup. Before you answer, say, "I need the same choice framed both ways."
extracts: Certainty has a special shine.
It moves when the frame moves.
Then the next act is to ask for the missing comparison, because a hidden reference point can steer the whole room.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice Name the Frame First before you accept a risky choice. Write the reference point, then mark whether the offer is being sold as a gain, a loss, or a sure thing. Put the common parts back beside the differences before you answer.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before your next commute or first coffee, move one current choice note beside your keys. Use it to rewrite the choice as a gain, a loss, and a sure thing.

chapter_evidence.title: The Rules of Undoing
chapter_evidence.hook: 5 minutes late, would you blame the missed flight or the one small delay you can replay?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Why does the same loss hurt more when one tiny change seems nearby? Because the mind does not just record what happened; it edits the scene it wishes had happened.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Regret follows a rule: when a nearby change is easy to picture, the outcome feels worse, even when the facts have not changed.
chapter_evidence.try: Within the next 24 hours, the first time regret replays a small edit, spend ten minutes counting each replay and write one handoff note: "Check the edit before the blame."
extracts: Anais watches a train delay crawl across the station board.
Ask for the nearby edit.
Then ask whether that edit could really carry the weight you are putting on it.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice catching the exact edit your mind replays after a bad outcome. Count the nearby edit by naming the small change, checking how easy it is to picture, and asking what else would have had to shift. The skill turns regret into evidence without letting a vivid story become the whole truth.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a near miss bothers you, count how many small edits your mind offers. Write the top edit in one handoff note for later.

chapter_evidence.title: This Cloud of Possibility
chapter_evidence.hook: I once trusted the prize photo; the missing partner taught the harder lesson.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The ending is not a repaired friendship, but a working method that outlived the hurt. In 2002, one name could receive the prize; the questions still carried two minds.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: When shared work outlives a damaged bond, keep both truths visible: name the hurt, then ask which question still helps people judge better.
chapter_evidence.try: Before you send your next reply, mark ? on a sticky note, count three claims in the thread, then write one line: What question should outlive my credit?
extracts: Every clean ending asks someone to pay for the shine.
Do it before the room decides that the prize alone explains the work.
You gain a cleaner view of what the work is still doing.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice the Surviving Question Line before you answer a claim about credit or legacy. Mark a small question on a surface you already see, count the claims in front of you, and write one line naming the question that should outlive praise or blame. The skill keeps hurt and usefulness in the same frame.
chapter_evidence.challenge: For the next day, mark ? on a sticky note before three replies about credit. Count the claims in each thread, then write one Surviving Question Line.
