chapter_evidence.title: Fully Engaged: Energy, Not Time, Is Our Most Precious Resource
chapter_evidence.hook: Which client call gets your best self after another late meal?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Full engagement is not a softer name for rest. It is the harder discipline of spending and renewing physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual energy on purpose.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Stop asking only how many hours remain. Ask which kind of energy the next demand needs, then spend and renew that capacity on purpose.
chapter_evidence.try: Before your next demanding moment, take ten seconds to name the energy it will need most: body, emotion, attention, or purpose. Choose one small renewal step before you begin.
extracts: At Harvard Business Review, the performance pyramid does not treat energy as one vague mood.
The claim is not that pressure is bad.
It does not fit someone looking for a prettier label for either overwork or escape.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice Check the Energy Leak before a demanding moment begins. Name the kind of energy the next demand needs, then choose one renewal step you can take before the demand starts. The check keeps the plan small enough to use under pressure without turning it into a display.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Today, before each demanding moment, run a ten-second Energy Leak Check: name body, emotion, attention, or purpose, then take one matching renewal step before you begin.

chapter_evidence.title: The Disengaged Life of Roger B.
chapter_evidence.hook: You can look busy enough that I once mistook depletion for drive.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Roger B. could be winning and shrinking at once: the work still got done while his capacity for home, health, and patience kept closing.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Disengagement drift starts when capacity leaks while output survives; name the gap, recover before promising more, and treat energy like trainable skill.
chapter_evidence.try: During your next conversation about a request, count two signs of flat energy, then write the exact reply you will use: "I can answer after I eat and reset."
extracts: Lisa spreads the week on a page before the new quarter begins.
Where is energy being spent without being renewed?
The earlier you name the capacity gap, the less you have to wait for a public failure to prove the private leak was real.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Run the Capacity Gap Check before you accept more work. Name the layer that is weakest: physical, emotional, mental, or spiritual. Then write the smallest honest promise that protects recovery and still respects the people affected.
chapter_evidence.challenge: For 24 hours, count the next three times a request lands while you feel depleted. Before replying, pre-write the exact words: "I can do this after I recover by ___."

chapter_evidence.title: The Pulse of High Performance: Balancing Stress and Recovery
chapter_evidence.hook: 2 clean breaks or one more hour: which protects your next best effort?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: What looks like easing off is actually training. The right pause is not a reward after work; it is part of the work that keeps capacity strong.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: The pulse beats the grind: spend energy hard, renew it on purpose, and let physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual capacity meet the next demand.
chapter_evidence.try: At your first coffee, before you open the busiest app, name today's hardest task and set one 90-to-120-minute work block with a real recovery break at the end.
extracts: A trading desk can make recovery look unserious.
He could spend energy hard because he had a way to get it back.
The aim is to spend energy on purpose and recover before the next demand gets the leftovers.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice placing recovery inside performance instead of after it. Build the Renewal Pulse by pairing a hard effort with a visible cue for renewal, then returning to the next demand with better state, not just more willpower.
chapter_evidence.challenge: For the next 24 hours, attach Build the Renewal Pulse to your laptop lid. When you close it after a hard block, take a real five-minute break before reopening: stand up, drink water, and look away from the screen.

chapter_evidence.title: Physical Energy: Fueling the Fire
chapter_evidence.hook: I used to think your body could wait backstage while ambition took the lights.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A tired body can look disciplined and still be stealing the next hour's judgment. Physical care is performance work when it renews usable capacity.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Treat physical energy as trainable fuel: spend it hard, renew it on purpose, and let sleep, food, water, and movement protect your best thinking.
chapter_evidence.try: Within the next 24 hours, the first time you reach for more push after a dip, write one recovery sentence and mark [ ] sleep [ ] water [ ] food. Then do one of them now: drink the water, eat something, or block tonight's sleep.
extracts: Ava fills a glass during a long afternoon and notices how ordinary the repair looks.
Yet the body is where serious work has to happen.
The practice is modest, but the promise is not: a better-fueled body gives your patience, focus, and care a fairer chance.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice spotting the first physical dip before you turn it into a character story. Mark the Renewal Loop asks for one visible check: what was spent, what input is missing, and what small refill comes next. The skill is not self-care talk; it is capacity training for the next decision.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a physical dip appears, do one real refill. Write one sentence naming the missing input, mark its check box, and take that input now: water, food, or a scheduled block of sleep.

chapter_evidence.title: Emotional Energy: Transforming Threat into Challenge
chapter_evidence.hook: A blinking reply box holds one sharp sentence; will it widen the moment or tighten it?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Despite how strong pressure can look from the outside, threat is a costly fuel. Challenge keeps effort useful without pretending the pressure is gone.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Emotional energy improves performance when you turn threat into challenge, spend it on what matters, and renew before pressure shrinks your options.
chapter_evidence.try: Before you send your next response, set a 75-second timer. Count three threat cues in the draft, then delete one sentence whose only job is to win.
extracts: A fire alarm is not a cue for reflection.
Eric can name a real problem and still refuse to answer from threat.
In those moments, challenge is disciplined fuel.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice turning threat into challenge before your next response. The move is to count visible threat cues, stop one defensive behavior, and send the line that protects the work or relationship. Use it when pressure is real but immediate safety is not at stake.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before each hard reply today, set a 75-second timer. Count the threat cues, stop one proof-seeking sentence, and send the clearest challenge line.

chapter_evidence.title: Mental Energy: Appropriate Focus and Realistic Optimism
chapter_evidence.hook: Have I ever called my scattered attention discipline when it was only strain?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: You may expect sharper focus to come from more strain. In fact, it often comes from rehearsing the aim, spending attention fully, then releasing it before fatigue scatters the mind.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Focused attention is trained energy: choose the target, rehearse the moment, renew before fatigue, and return with realistic optimism.
chapter_evidence.try: The next time you feel the pull to check everything, do not open the first tab. Write one line: I am training attention for ____.
extracts: Tate reads the diving story and wants to make it a productivity trick.
That is the shallow use of mental energy.
Focus needs a finish line.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice turning scattered attention into a written target before pressure spends it for you. Use the Write the Focus Cue move: name the task, picture one concrete action, then release when the burst is done. The skill is not constant concentration; it is the trained return.
chapter_evidence.challenge: The next time you feel the pull to check everything, write one Focus Cue line: I am training attention for ____. Do the named first move before opening another input.

chapter_evidence.title: Spiritual Energy: He Who Has a Why
chapter_evidence.hook: You are at the next handoff; which yes will protect the value you say comes first?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Why does purpose sometimes make the strong move smaller? A real why gives energy a target, so it may ask you to drop one demand before you add one more effort.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Purpose becomes energy when a chosen value decides what you endure, refuse, recover for, and protect before raw effort spends you down.
chapter_evidence.try: At your next handoff between tasks, write one sentence naming the value you protect, say it aloud, then remove one small ask that steals from it.
extracts: Richard reached the park before home and let the last ten blocks change him.
Purpose also needs truth.
The stronger practice is simpler: name the value, pay the right cost, and stop paying costs that do not belong to it.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice turning a vague why into a receipt you can test. Name the value, name the demand you will drop or keep, and say what energy the value deserves next. The skill is small on purpose: purpose has to change one handoff before it can change a life.
chapter_evidence.challenge: For one workday, at the next handoff between tasks, say one Purpose Receipt sentence aloud before accepting the next demand. Cut one small ask that does not serve the named value.

chapter_evidence.title: Defining Purpose: The Rules of Engagement
chapter_evidence.hook: 3 steps from your door, your workday may still be choosing how you treat the people inside.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Purpose is not a fine sentence about what matters, but a rule that gets a vote when pressure starts bargaining.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Purpose becomes useful when a value gains authority over a repeated choice, and recovery gives the body enough fuel to keep that choice.
chapter_evidence.try: Before your next threshold, write your purpose rule as one named cue and one fixed threshold ("when X, I do Y"). Read it aloud, then name 4 pressures that would try to bargain it away.
extracts: Brett can make purpose sound impressive and still leave the day untouched.
A purpose rule that ignores emotion turns harsh.
Purpose works best when there is enough ground under the feet to practice it.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice turning one value into one rule for a repeated moment. Write the Purpose Rule asks you to name what matters, find where it gets lost, and attach one visible behavior to that threshold.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before your next threshold, write one purpose rule as a fixed cue-and-threshold ("when X, I do Y"). Read it aloud, name the first 4 pressures that would bargain it away, and obey the rule once.

chapter_evidence.title: Face the Truth: How Are You Managing Your Energy Now?
chapter_evidence.hook: Where do I spend my best energy before I admit the day is already overdrawn?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The audit hurts and helps at once: it names the deficit so capacity can be trained instead of defended.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A truthful energy audit turns exhaustion into data: count where capacity leaks, then renew the body, mood, focus, and purpose that performance uses.
chapter_evidence.try: During your next conversation about a strained moment, do not defend your schedule first. Count each urge to explain before you name the energy cost.
extracts: Ruby records a voice memo before the Energy Audit review and predicts the result will be obvious.
A truthful energy audit does not fix all four layers at once.
Once the crisis passes, the count can tell her what the crisis cost.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice Run the Energy Truth Count before you redesign anything. Count where your body, mood, focus, and purpose were actually spent in one real situation. The skill is not self-blame; it is clean measurement before change.
chapter_evidence.challenge: During your next conversation about a strained moment, do not explain your schedule first. Count each urge to defend, then write the energy cost you noticed.

chapter_evidence.title: Taking Action: The Power of Positive Rituals
chapter_evidence.hook: I used to walk into hard meetings with my pulse already writing the script.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: What looks like a small routine is actually performance design: cue, action, timing, and recovery chosen before pressure starts.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Positive rituals turn intent into repeatable conduct by tying a clear cue to one small action, then protecting recovery before pressure bargains it away.
chapter_evidence.try: At the next doorway into work, write START on a sticky note. Name one action that begins the mode you want before pressure writes it for you.
extracts: A vague ritual can become another way to fail.
The ritual does not erase nerves.
Then add another only when the first one still helps under strain.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice naming the cue that starts the conduct you want. Use Name The Start Line: choose the threshold, write the first action, and protect the renewal that keeps the ritual from becoming strain. The skill is precision under pressure, not adding more chores.
chapter_evidence.challenge: For the next workday, put START on one surface you already see. Each time you cross into a new work mode, say the cue and do the first action before checking inputs.

chapter_evidence.title: The Reengaged Life of Roger B.
chapter_evidence.hook: Can a full calendar look calmer and still be draining the person who carries it?
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Roger B. can leave the office earlier and still be unrecovered if his body, mood, focus, and purpose are not working as one system.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Reengagement is trained integration: spend energy on purpose, renew it on purpose, and let routines connect body, emotion, focus, and values.
chapter_evidence.try: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a task crowds out recovery, count three barriers to a short reset. Remove one, then pre-write: "I will restart after ten clear breaths."
extracts: Florence hears the phrase energy management and wants one clean fix.
A shorter drain from work helped the evening.
Rituals cannot repair a lie about where energy goes.
examples: Shannon and Marie Name the Design
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Practice linking one energy move to the next demand. Before you add a routine, name the layer it renews and the next layer it should help. The move is not to do more self-care; it is to build a chain that makes performance recoverable.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a demand threatens recovery, count four visible friction points. Remove one, then pre-write the words you will use: "I can do this after I renew."

chapter_evidence.title: Should Have Been a Statistic
chapter_evidence.hook: A childhood file can explain the wound without earning the right to command the next move.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The visible damage looks like the abuse, the poverty, the missed schooling. In fact, the real damage is the old rule still voting in a room where the danger left years ago.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Tell the truth about the damage, then remove its authority over the next action; history can explain the wound without running the day.
chapter_evidence.try: Write one hard fact from your past as evidence, then write the next present action beside it that the fact does not get to cancel.
extracts: A county survivor benefits office is a bad place to learn courage.
The form still asks for the next appointment.
It cannot leave as the sentence.
examples: Sloane Slides the Report into the Tray
Daniel Signs the Gate Log Before Midnight
Claire Crosses Out the Old Address
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to keep two truths in the same room: the damage was real, and the next action still belongs to you. The work is to inventory the wound without making it the manager of the day.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one past fact that still gets a vote. Write it in one sentence, then complete one small action today that proves it no longer has veto power.

chapter_evidence.title: Truth Hurts
chapter_evidence.hook: A fogged mirror becomes useful only when the lie on it is replaced by a task.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Confession gets the credit. Counterintuitively, the calendar block is doing the work, because a posted truth has to answer to tomorrow's rep.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A hard truth changes you only when it becomes a visible assignment with a deadline, not when it becomes another feeling to manage.
chapter_evidence.try: Write the one fact you keep softening, then add a deadline and a proof of work that another person could check.
extracts: Graham opens his fire academy locker and finds the red failed-score sheet under his gloves.
Exposure says, look how bad I am.
Truth on the wall starts charging rent.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to turn a private ugly fact into a posted assignment. The test is whether the truth changes your calendar, checklist, or trigger before shame has time to hide it again.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Name one fact you have been softening. Put it beside a date, then complete the first proof of work within the next day.

chapter_evidence.title: The Impossible Task
chapter_evidence.hook: A deadline sharp enough to scare you can turn a wish into a bill that comes due tomorrow.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Why does a brutal deadline help more than a clear plan, despite the plan looking like the safer bet? Because the deadline forces the old life to name what it will lose, while a clear plan can stay clean while the body refuses.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A mission becomes real when its deadline and cost are clear enough to rewrite tomorrow's behavior, not just excite today's mood.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one goal you keep admiring from a distance, then write the first deadline, first cost, and first thing you must cancel.
extracts: Blake's truck smells like chemical gloves and stale drive-through fries.
There is a danger here.
A mission starts moving things out.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to turn a goal into a priced mission. The proof is not how intense the target sounds, but whether the deadline and cost force a concrete change in the next twenty-four hours.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Write one admired goal as a mission invoice: deadline, standard, first cost, and one comfort you will cancel before tomorrow night.

chapter_evidence.title: Taking Souls
chapter_evidence.hook: A soaked plank lifted in silence can change the whole crew's idea of who is breaking first.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: When the smaller fighter looks like he has no chance, the move is the opposite of brave talk: choose a narrow place where pace, timing, or pain can turn the larger opponent's size into a tax on him.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Under shared pressure, relentless visible effort can shift morale; use it to raise the standard, not to turn toughness into cruelty.
chapter_evidence.try: In the next shared hard task, choose one visible next action that answers the room's doubt without a speech, then do it first.
extracts: The marina smells like diesel, mud, and torn wood.
Who is your effort serving when people watch it?
Let the room feel the pressure shift.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to use visible effort as a pressure signal in shared hardship. The skill is to move first in a way that serves the standard, while keeping contempt and performance out of it.
chapter_evidence.challenge: During one shared hard task today, choose a visible next action and do it before speaking about morale.

chapter_evidence.title: Armored Mind
chapter_evidence.hook: A cracked metronome beside a rehab chart tells a harder truth than a comeback speech.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The weak version of armor wants nothing to land. The strong version trains for what does, so the return after the hit takes minutes instead of weeks.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Armor is built by returning to the exposed point with a controlled drill, not by pretending injury, fear, or humiliation never landed.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one setback you keep treating as a verdict, then design the smallest return drill that touches the exposed point honestly.
extracts: Emily's recital notice is folded twice beside the piano, as if making it smaller will make the cancellation smaller too.
The mind works the same way.
It is the map of where the next layer has to be built.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to build durability through accurate return. The skill is naming the point a setback exposed, then touching it again at a dose that trains rather than denies.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one setback you keep avoiding. Build a return drill that touches the exact failed point for less than ten minutes today.

chapter_evidence.title: It's Not About a Trophy
chapter_evidence.hook: A chilled blood cooler at a closed ramp asks for a reason bigger than finishing first.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Despite the trophy carrying a name, it stops moving the legs once exhaustion gets honest. Duty is what keeps the next step on the road long after pride goes quiet.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: When the body asks for a smaller reason, stored proof and service can keep the next step connected to duty instead of applause.
chapter_evidence.try: Write one proof that you have endured something hard before, then tie today's next hard action to a duty beyond your own credit.
extracts: The snow has turned the highway ramp into a white wall.
When proof is not enough, reach for duty.
Then take the next step that duty actually requires.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to pair stored proof with a duty beyond credit. The skill is not to glorify suffering, but to keep the next step connected to someone or something that still matters when comfort starts bargaining.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Write one hard thing you have already completed and one person or duty served by today's next hard action. Do the action at a safe, bounded scale.

chapter_evidence.title: The Most Powerful Weapon
chapter_evidence.hook: A warning light in a simulator can be panic, danger, or a checklist asking to be finished.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Quitting gets blamed on weakness. Often it is a misread signal: fatigue treated as verdict instead of pacing data, and the pause to inspect it changes the next mile.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Your first limit may be a protective signal, so test it with pacing and judgment before treating it as final or fake.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one hard stop signal from today. Write the body fact, the fear story, and one controlled test that would tell you which one is true.
extracts: Olivia hears the warning tone in the simulator and feels her hands turn clumsy on the throttle.
It is a signal.
Then let the next measured step give you better evidence than the first frightened sentence.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to inspect the first stop signal before treating it as a verdict. The skill is choosing a measured next step that gives better information without turning toughness into denial.
chapter_evidence.challenge: When one stop signal appears today, write danger, pacing, or bargaining beside it. Choose one measured next step only after that label.

chapter_evidence.title: Talent Not Required
chapter_evidence.hook: A route map under cooler logs can prove that harder work is not the missing piece.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Hard work can hide bad process, but the review has to honor effort without protecting it from evidence. The useful move is not blame; instead, it is naming the exact handoff, map, or timing failure before pride edits the tape.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Grit still matters, but underperformance often asks for better logistics and tactics before it asks for more suffering.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one recent miss. Write the intended result, the actual result, the first broken handoff, and the next visible checkpoint.
extracts: Natalie has two cold-chain records pinned over the county route map, and the ink on the missed-stop circles has bled through the paper.
The team worked hard.
Read it before you push harder.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to protect effort from waste. The skill is reviewing underperformance for the route, fuel, timing, handoff, or sequence that must change before intensity rises.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one area where you plan to try harder. Write the missing route, timing, handoff, or sequence that would let the next effort land.

chapter_evidence.title: Uncommon Amongst Uncommon
chapter_evidence.hook: A tangled beacon harness is a better leadership test than another display of strength.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Hoarding the rep feels like proof of excellence. The opposite is closer to true: standards stay rare only when one more person can carry them, so the next holder is the test.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Uncommon performance serves best when it gives others steadiness under pressure instead of becoming a private monument to superiority.
chapter_evidence.try: In the next room where you are stronger than someone else, use that edge to make their next step steadier, not your status louder.
extracts: Andrew could make the rookie feel it.
Uncommon is not the medal if nobody else can use the standard.
It is the responsibility that starts after the medal stops impressing you.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to turn uncommon ability into usable steadiness for others. The skill is keeping the standard high while making the next step clearer for someone under pressure.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Find one place where you are ahead of someone else. Use that edge to make their next step clearer without mentioning your advantage.

chapter_evidence.title: The Empowerment of Failure
chapter_evidence.hook: A failed score sheet dusted with flour has no wisdom until the weak line is circled.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Even though pain feels like the teacher, failure teaches only after subtraction, when the excuse story leaves the page and the missed standard sits on the bench with a corrected rep ready.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Failure becomes power only when ego gives up the story and the miss turns into a correction against the standard.
chapter_evidence.try: Take one recent miss and write the failed standard, the factual cause, and the correction you will rehearse before retrying.
extracts: Camille's score sheet is dusted with flour near the chilled marble slab.
First, name the standard.
If you cannot name the correction, you are not ready to call the failure useful.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to make failure operational. The skill is removing the story that protects your ego until the failed standard, factual cause, and rehearsed correction are visible.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one recent miss. Write the failed standard, the factual cause, and the correction you will rehearse before trying again.

chapter_evidence.title: What If?
chapter_evidence.hook: A dusty welding hood beside a mobility card asks a question force cannot answer.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Force gets the credit for the comeback. In fact, the final edge is repair: the discipline to honor the diagnosis, the daily mobility card, and the recoveries nobody counts.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: When proving is no longer enough, disciplined stillness and repair can open the next question without turning the ending soft.
chapter_evidence.try: Ask one hard what if about the part of your life that no longer responds to force, then write the smallest truthful repair action.
extracts: Arthur sets the welding hood on the bench and watches dust slide down the visor.
What if I stretch instead of boast?
A forward-looking question is only strong when it changes the next small act.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: You learn to keep discipline when the work shifts from proving to repair. The skill is asking a forward-looking question that produces one truthful recovery, transfer, or reconciliation action.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Ask one hard what if about the area where force no longer works. Write the smallest repair action and complete it today.

chapter_evidence.title: The Three Voices Inside You
chapter_evidence.hook: The dosage question is simple until the nurse's answer changes voices halfway through.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The fastest read comes before personality judgment. Listen for the state speaking right now, because a grown adult can move from Adult fact to Parent rule before one sentence is finished.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Before you answer the words, hear the ego state behind them: Parent rules, Adult data, or Child feeling will each pull a different reply from you.
chapter_evidence.try: Replay one tense sentence from today. Mark only its state: Parent rule, Adult data, or Child reaction. Leave the solution alone for now.
extracts: You are holding your phone above the counter while three gray dots pulse in the family chat.
A person is not "a Parent" or "a Child." They are in a state for a moment.
A clean next sentence often begins with hearing who was about to speak.
examples: Camille Points to the Cart Drop
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Learn to hear the state before answering the content. Parent, Adult, and Child each ask for a different kind of reply, and the conversation changes when you answer the wrong one.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one tense sentence you heard today. Write P, A, or C beside it, then write the reply you would give if you answered from Adult.

chapter_evidence.title: What a Transaction Is and Why They Go Wrong
chapter_evidence.hook: The outage thread breaks when a status question receives a courtroom answer.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A conversation can fail even when both sentences are clear. The break often sits in the arrow: one state was addressed, and a different state answered.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A transaction is one social move and one response; when the expected ego state answers, talk continues, and when another state answers, the subject breaks.
chapter_evidence.try: Draw two arrows for one exchange that went sideways. Label the state you addressed, then the state that answered. Do not add motives yet.
extracts: The microscope room hums behind a keypad that has locked three students out.
He got a rule answer.
It may be broken because the answer came from a state nobody addressed.
examples: James Keeps the Rollback Thread Open
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Learn to draw the exchange before fixing it. One sentence is the stimulus, the next is the response, and the useful question is which ego states were involved.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one exchange that went sideways today. Draw the sent arrow and returned arrow, then label each as Parent, Adult, or Child.

chapter_evidence.title: Ulterior Transactions and the Anatomy of a Game
chapter_evidence.hook: The compliment lands softly, but Claire can feel the invoice hidden inside it.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The surface sentence may be polite while the working message asks for surrender. Read both levels before you accept the role being offered.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A game begins when a visible exchange carries a hidden invitation and repeats toward a familiar payoff that both sides know how to reach.
chapter_evidence.try: Write one polite sentence you heard recently. Under it, write the possible hidden invitation in five words or fewer.
extracts: The yellow note curls at one corner on the refrigerator door: "Some of us clean shared spaces without needing reminders." Grace stands beside an overflowing recycling bin, a lemon-shaped magnet, and the cleaning rota no one has opened in a week.
A housemate note becomes grievance.
Sometimes the first freedom is to leave that part unplayed.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Learn to hear the polite sentence and the hidden invitation separately. You are not guessing motive for sport; you are checking whether the exchange is asking you to accept a role.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one polite request that felt loaded. Write the visible request on one line and the possible hidden invitation on the next.

chapter_evidence.title: Why Games Feel So Hard to Stop
chapter_evidence.hook: The warehouse gripe circle is bad for the shift, and still it feeds the room.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: It looks like the argument is the problem, but the supply is often the real hook. Replace the recognition before you remove the route, or the old route will look useful again by Friday.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Before trying to stop a game, identify what it provides; replacement has to come before exit or deprivation will pull the pattern back.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one recurring irritation. Name the supply it delivers: recognition, structure, escape, or proof of an old position.
extracts: Chlorine hangs in the pool lobby while Megan's child ties one wet shoelace.
It can still buy five minutes of contact.
First, find what the game has been feeding and put something less costly in its place.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Learn to ask what the pattern supplies before trying to remove it. The old exchange may be painful and still be feeding recognition, structure, avoidance, or position proof.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one recurring irritation and write the supply it provides in four words or fewer: recognition, structure, escape, or position proof.

chapter_evidence.title: Life Games
chapter_evidence.hook: The missing permit attachment is small enough to fix and large enough to prove a life story.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Long-running games are rarely solved by naming them at full volume. The cleaner move is to refuse your assigned role while respecting the real problem in front of you.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A life game is a repeated sequence that confirms an old position; refuse the role with neutral precision, not accusation.
chapter_evidence.try: When a recurring life pattern appears, write the payoff sentence it proves. Then write the smallest neutral refusal of your usual role.
extracts: You hear the word temporary for the fifth time before Petra's account screen finishes loading.
Kick Me asks you not to kick.
The next time the familiar scene offers you your old role, answer the visible problem precisely and leave the role on the floor.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Learn to refuse the role, not the person. Life games are costly because they confirm old positions over time, so the clean move handles the visible problem without supplying the expected payoff.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Find one recurring life scene you know too well. Write the role you usually play, then write one neutral sentence that refuses only that role.

chapter_evidence.title: Marital Games
chapter_evidence.hook: Six flooring samples can become a maze when every choice proves the same accusation.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The fight often protects the couple from the closer question. Who wins the flooring, the verdict, or the apology can matter less than what contact the game helps both people avoid.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Relationship games preserve distance by making familiar roles feel necessary; refuse the structure by naming the shared constraint instead of prosecuting the partner.
chapter_evidence.try: Name the safer role a relationship argument keeps giving you: judge, defendant, rescuer, restricted one, martyr, or harmless joker.
extracts: It took Emily until deadline week to notice the nursing-school application tab had been open for six weeks.
The task is not to prove one partner false.
The better test is whether the next sentence makes closeness more possible or gives everyone a cleaner excuse to stay in role.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Learn to identify the role a relationship game keeps handing you. The better response is usually a concrete constraint, question, or agreement that makes direct contact more possible.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Name one repeated relationship role you step into. Write the shared constraint or checkable ask that would make the role less necessary.

chapter_evidence.title: Party and Social Games
chapter_evidence.hook: The leaking lobby gives the parents a real complaint and a very comfortable circle.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Shared complaint can look like honesty, but it becomes a game when it refuses movement. Test direction: does the exchange open toward action, contact, or curiosity?
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Short social games turn complaint, critique, and advice into predictable strokes; break them by asking whether the talk moves anywhere.
chapter_evidence.try: During the next group complaint, ask one action question: what would we do for ten minutes if we meant this?
extracts: "What about a short sublet near the train?" Olivia types into the group chat.
It is another way to be first with the flaw.
If the talk resents the exit, you have found the game.
examples: Laura Asks for the Leak Photo
Etienne Stops at the Bid Flaw
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Learn to test direction in short social exchanges. The aim is not to condemn complaint or critique; it is to notice when the exchange refuses movement because the familiar payoff is the point.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In one group complaint today, ask a single action question and watch whether the group moves, pauses, or resists the exit.

chapter_evidence.title: Professional and Therapy-Room Games
chapter_evidence.hook: The third referral looks generous until Rebecca hears how useful its failure would be.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The professional role can hide the helper's payoff. Look at both sides of the exchange before deciding who is stuck and who is benefiting from stuckness.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Helping games stay respectable because help is visible; test whether the offer has a usable path or needs failure to prove the helper tried.
chapter_evidence.try: Before offering help again, write what would count as the other person using it. If you cannot name that, pause the offer.
extracts: The accessibility office window faces a courtyard full of construction noise.
The quiz requirement is also real.
If no one can say what using the help would look like, the offer may already be part of the game.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Learn to make help testable. A professional role can hide the helper's payoff, so both sides need a visible path for what using the help would mean.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Before your next offer of help, write the sentence: This help will be used if blank. Fill in the blank with a visible action.

chapter_evidence.title: Games That Aren't Worth Fighting
chapter_evidence.hook: The clinic kitchen smells like onions, fatigue, and one mixed motive doing useful work.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Mixed motives do not automatically spoil a pattern. Some social games are worth leaving alone because the contribution is larger than the private reward.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A good game may still be ulterior and imperfect; leave it alone when it helps more than it costs and does not need anyone stuck.
chapter_evidence.try: Before interrupting a mixed-motive pattern, ask three questions: who benefits, who is trapped, and does this require failure?
extracts: Sticker-covered laptops glow under a basketball hoop in the school gym.
The students own the skill.
Protect the generosity inside them.
examples: Chris Lets the Bug Fix Teach
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Learn to evaluate mixed motives by effects. Some patterns are technically games and still worth protecting because they feed, teach, help, or admire without trapping anyone.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Notice one mixed-motive good act today. Ask who benefits, who is trapped, and whether the act needs failure to continue.

chapter_evidence.title: What Comes After Games
chapter_evidence.hook: The red pen cap clicks shut, and Audrey notices the old sentence before it uses her mouth.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Freedom after games is not constant calm or isolation, but the ability to notice the prepared move, choose from a wider range, and meet someone without a hidden payoff.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Autonomy is the direction after games: awareness, spontaneity, and intimacy used as living capacities, not as another performance.
chapter_evidence.try: In one conversation today, catch the prepared line before it leaves your mouth. Take one breath, then answer only what is present.
extracts: Soot dries in the creases of every hand around the debrief table.
Intimacy is rare because one person cannot produce it alone.
It is the moment you can leave the game unplayed.
examples: Antoine Laughs at the Wrong Note
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Use awareness, spontaneity, and intimacy as direction markers. Do not convert them into another role to perform.
chapter_evidence.challenge: In the next real conversation, catch one prepared line, breathe once, and answer the situation actually in front of you.

chapter_evidence.title: Becoming Limitless
chapter_evidence.hook: Under the lab light, the old label sounds convincing until the red string moves.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: The painful limit is not the whole problem. The larger trap is treating repeated struggle as a verdict instead of asking which process has never been trained.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A felt limit can be real without being final; the useful move is to test the learning process before obeying the old label.
chapter_evidence.try: Write one label you still carry from learning badly, then turn it into one process question you can test before tomorrow night.
extracts: Ingrid smells chlorine before she hears anyone speak.
They are a practice map.
One small test begins before the old story can close the file again.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Turn a painful learning label into a process test. The skill is naming the exact cue, method, or condition that failed before deciding what the failure says about you. Confidence can come later; the first job is to move the problem where practice can reach it.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one old label from school, work, or home. Write the smallest observable process behind it and run one test of that process before tomorrow night.

chapter_evidence.title: Why This Matters Now
chapter_evidence.hook: Storm alerts blink all night while the one card Claire must remember stays face down.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Overload feels like proof that you need more input. The stronger response is triage: decide what must be recalled, what can be referenced, and what should be ignored.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Modern cognitive pressure rewards learners who sort information by use before attention gets spent.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose one incoming stream today. Mark each item as recall, file, or ignore. Then learn only the recall pile.
extracts: Daniel sits at a local news election desk with red correction tape across the rundown sheet.
The risk is pretending this is only about work.
For Claire, the difference shows up before the storm shift begins: one triage card in memory, one reference shelf for the rest, and fewer alerts pretending to deserve the same treatment.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Sort information by use before attention gets spent. Identify what must be held in memory, what only needs a reliable home, and what can be ignored — then learn only the recall pile. This skill protects working memory in any environment where updates and alerts compete for the same limited attention.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one incoming information stream today and mark each item R, F, or I before reading any item in full. Then spend study time only on the R pile.

chapter_evidence.title: Your Limitless Brain
chapter_evidence.hook: Middle C sounds different on Friday because Vera kept the Monday recording.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A weak performance can feel permanent, but one discouraged snapshot is not a capacity test. Method, feedback, and repetition reveal what can move.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Current performance is a snapshot; trainable capacity shows up only after the conditions around practice change.
chapter_evidence.try: Pick one skill that feels fixed and create a before-and-after check: record today, train one condition, compare again in a week.
extracts: Pablo stands over a heritage bakery scale with cinnamon stuck to the pan.
One failed batch gives information.
That question keeps hope useful and keeps denial out of the room.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Test capacity through comparison, not through first impressions. The skill is separating a current snapshot from a final range by changing one practice condition and checking whether the result moves. Discouragement is treated as a prompt to measure, not as a verdict.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one skill that feels fixed. Record or measure your performance today, then identify one practice condition to change. Set a date to compare.

chapter_evidence.title: How to Read and Remember This (and Any) Book
chapter_evidence.hook: Yellow tabs look busy until Emily closes the casebook and says the holding aloud.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Finishing pages can masquerade as learning. Reading becomes useful when the mind must retrieve, explain, or use the point before the text disappears.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Active reading turns exposure into recall, so the page has to become usable before the eyes move on.
chapter_evidence.try: After the next paragraph, close the page and say the point aloud in one plain sentence before you keep reading.
extracts: Tomas sits in a city bus training room with a folded route map on the vinyl driver's seat.
What will you need to do with this after the page is gone?
That makes repair possible while the page is still nearby and the purpose is still clear.
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Turn reading into retrieval by closing the text before testing yourself. The skill is creating a small demand — say it, sketch it, explain it — that forces the material to leave the page and enter memory. Exposure gets the ground ready; retrieval is what plants the seed.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Read the next thing on your study list. After each section, close the source and write the main point from memory before opening the next section.

chapter_evidence.title: The Spell of Belief Systems
chapter_evidence.hook: Olivia has the sales sheet open before the old number story can shut it.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A belief feels private, yet it changes public behavior. The hidden ceiling is the task you avoid before ability has been tested.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A limiting belief has power when it edits effort before reality has had a chance to answer.
chapter_evidence.try: Find one sentence that begins with I am bad at, then name the exact action it keeps you from starting.
extracts: Marco holds a nonprofit grant budget with one red circle around a term he hates.
The belief does not vanish.
The better proof is what happens when the learner finally runs the small test the belief kept postponing.
examples: Olivia Opens the Sales Sheet Anyway
Astrid Lines Up the Glaze Tests
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Name the belief that is editing effort before ability gets tested, then find the smallest action that forces the belief to face evidence. The skill is not positive thinking — it is getting something done before the old story can close the file.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one task you have been avoiding because of a belief about your ability. Do the smallest possible version of it today — before confidence arrives.

chapter_evidence.title: The 7 Lies of Learning
chapter_evidence.hook: The housing portal waits while Sophie asks what the myth is making impossible.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A learning myth is dangerous because it gives passivity a respectable excuse. Judge the belief by the behavior it produces.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Bad learning myths should be tested by their consequences: what they prevent, delay, or make needlessly intimidating.
chapter_evidence.try: Name one learning myth you repeat, then write the action it blocks and one test that would make the myth answerable.
extracts: Thomas holds a craft brewery sample tube with foam residue still clinging to the glass.
Learning should be fast.
If it blocks a renewal click, a question, a card, or a tray, it has become part of the problem.
examples: Henrik Writes the Question on the Work Order
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Identify the learning belief and test it by the behavior it produces. The skill is catching the moment when a myth is making avoidance look reasonable — and choosing the direct, somewhat awkward action the myth was blocking.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Find one learning myth you currently hold. Ask what behavior it is producing today and whether that behavior is helping or blocking your progress.

chapter_evidence.title: Purpose
chapter_evidence.hook: The tissue box beside Laura’s practice card changes what the script is for.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Motivation fades when it depends on mood alone. Purpose gives effort a person, promise, or future room to serve.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Purpose turns effort from a mood-dependent task into chosen direction tied to something that matters.
chapter_evidence.try: Write the name of the person or future situation served by today’s learning task at the top of the page.
extracts: Antoine spreads flashcards beside a turnout coat before the firefighter academy exam.
Purpose has limits.
Purpose helps decide which discomfort is worth carrying and which one is only noise.
examples: Laura Names the Person in the Room
Mikkel Links the Code to the Job Site
Giulia Links the Audition to Her Daughter
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Anchor effort to a specific person, promise, or future moment before the work begins. Purpose replaces mood as the engine by making difficulty accountable to something that does not change when feelings do.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one task you have been avoiding. Write the name of one person or the description of one future moment this task serves, place it where you can see it, and begin.

chapter_evidence.title: Energy
chapter_evidence.hook: Flour fingerprints on the steel table tell Megan the recipe is not the only problem.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Low energy can disguise itself as weak character. Before blaming commitment, check whether the mind has enough fuel to learn.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Motivation needs energy underneath it; exhaustion can distort attention before effort has a fair chance.
chapter_evidence.try: Before the next hard learning block, check fuel first. Write one note for sleep, food, movement, and timing; adjust the weakest one.
extracts: Javier stands beside lettuce crates sweating under an urban farm shade tarp.
Energy is a condition, not a character verdict.
Only then is a harsher conclusion worth considering.
examples: Megan Moves the Drill to a Fueled Hour
Anders Moves Study Before the Shift
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Diagnose energy conditions before judging effort or character. The skill is noticing when poor performance correlates with depleted resources — food, sleep, timing — and designing practice around the conditions that produce the best work.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Identify one learning task you have been struggling with. Check the energy conditions around your last three attempts. Design the next attempt for your best energy window with food and rest in place.

chapter_evidence.title: Small Simple Steps
chapter_evidence.hook: One cream envelope on the scanner is less frightening than the whole probate box.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: A big goal can create resistance by making the start too expensive. Shrink the entry until action can happen before confidence arrives.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: A small simple step lowers the cost of starting without pretending the larger goal is easy.
chapter_evidence.try: Choose the task you are avoiding and place only the first physical object needed for the next move in front of you.
extracts: Niklas kneels by an apartment door with a rolled rubber sweep, a utility bill, and a screwdriver.
Then the next step can be larger.
Warm air still leaks at the window, so the first step has done its proper job: it has named the second one.
examples: Isabel Knocks on the Blue Door
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Lower the entry cost of any task by naming the smallest possible concrete first action. The skill is identifying the one move that makes starting less expensive than avoiding — then doing it before confidence or planning is complete.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Pick one task you have been avoiding. Find the smallest possible first step — something you can do in under five minutes — and do it today before planning anything else.

chapter_evidence.title: Flow
chapter_evidence.hook: Orange glass gathers at the pipe when Alice chooses a challenge that can hold her.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Flow is not frantic speed or easy pleasure. It appears when challenge is demanding enough to absorb attention without tipping into panic.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Flow grows from a fit between challenge and skill, where attention can enter the task instead of fleeing it.
chapter_evidence.try: Take one task and adjust it one notch: add challenge if bored, reduce scope if panicked, then work until attention steadies.
extracts: David adjusts a softbox over a sleeping newborn blanket while parents wait through the only calm hour.
Flow is not the only valuable mode.
It is whether the glass keeps asking for the next careful turn.
examples: Alice Chooses the Form Just Beyond Comfort
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Tune the challenge level of a task until it demands full attention without triggering panic. The skill is reading when you are bored versus when you are panicked, and adjusting difficulty — not duration or effort — to restore fit.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one practice or work task for today. Ask: is this boring or panicking me? Adjust the difficulty — up or down — until it requires genuine attention, then begin.

chapter_evidence.title: Focus
chapter_evidence.hook: Two grayscale scans wait in the dim room while the pager asks to own the minute.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Focus is less about stern effort than about closing the competing pull before it taxes comprehension.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Protected attention lets learning stay clean by blocking the switch before it fragments the work.
chapter_evidence.try: Before one learning block today, remove the single pull most likely to interrupt it and finish one unit before reopening it.
extracts: Ben marks a tenor entrance on the choir score while a parent-message thread lights up his phone.
The scan comparison needs one protected loop.
Ben answers the parent thread after the score markings are done, so focus serves the choir without pretending the messages do not matter.
examples: Lukas Closes Every Tab But One
Paula Completes One Code Decision End to End
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Close the competing pull before the work begins instead of relying on willpower to ignore it during the session. Focus is an environmental gate: design the space so that attention can stay inside the task without spending effort on resistance.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one task that demands accuracy today. Before starting, identify every competing pull — notifications, tabs, people, devices — and close or silence each one. Work for one uninterrupted block and compare the result to a typical session.

chapter_evidence.title: Study
chapter_evidence.hook: The canine skeleton on the cart exposes what Kate only recognized on paper.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Familiarity can feel like understanding while the answer is visible, but study works only when exposure becomes retrieval, explanation, or use.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Strong study makes the learner do something with the material instead of only meeting it again.
chapter_evidence.try: Cover the answer after one study item and either point, explain, or choose before checking yourself.
extracts: Chris sits in a union contract reading group with article nine creased under his thumb.
A decision tree.
The question is not whether the page looked familiar; the question is what the learner can make, choose, explain, or repair after the page closes.
examples: Kate Tests the Skeleton Without Labels
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Make the material act before trusting that you have learned it. The skill is building a demand into every study session — point to it, decide with it, explain it, rebuild it — so that understanding must be proved by production instead of assumed from familiarity.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Choose one topic you have been reading about. Close all sources and write everything you can produce from memory. Compare against the source. The gaps are your actual study list.

chapter_evidence.title: Memory
chapter_evidence.hook: Ivory place cards spread beside the phone before Lucy lets a detail vanish.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Memory is often treated as a gift after the fact. Better recall begins while the material is still warm enough to encode, connect, and retrieve.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Memory improves when you build a retrieval path early instead of hoping exposure will harden on its own.
chapter_evidence.try: Take one fact you need later, attach it to a vivid cue in the room, and retrieve it once with the cue covered.
extracts: Jack turns a laminated protocol card face down in paramedic class.
That is memory as method.
Lucy does not memorize every vendor note; she builds a retrieval path for allergies, timing, and calls that must be correct while the reception is moving.
examples: Matteo Walks the Route Before the Drill
Hanna Connects Each Name to One Preference
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Build a retrieval path before the material cools. The skill is giving each important piece of information a concrete hook — location, image, sequence, connection — and then practicing retrieval from that hook before the real test arrives.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Take one piece of important information you need to remember. Create a concrete hook for it — a location, an image, a connection — and retrieve it from the hook three times today before closing the source.

chapter_evidence.title: Speed Reading
chapter_evidence.hook: Ruth’s finger moves quickly until the outcome table asks for a slower mind.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: Reading faster is not the same as skimming harder; pace routine text quickly, then slow down where comprehension changes the decision.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Speed reading works only when pace serves comprehension, reducing friction without flattening every text.
chapter_evidence.try: Preview one page, mark where you can pace quickly and where you must slow, then read with those two speeds on purpose.
extracts: Anke works through a public-comment packet in the planning office, three hundred pages of resident letters clipped in stacks.
Your speed should change at that border.
Speed earns trust when it protects that turn instead of flattening it.
examples: Ruth Slows Down at the Outcome Table
You Stop When the Claim Overlaps Your Design
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Allocate reading pace based on where the text changes a decision. Move quickly through familiar structure and boilerplate; slow fully where comprehension affects what you do next. The skill is making the pace decision before reading each section, not reacting after confusion arrives.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Read one document today at variable pace: preview the headings, mark where the text is likely to change your decision, then read that section slowly and move through the rest at a higher pace.

chapter_evidence.title: Thinking
chapter_evidence.hook: Tracing paper over the zoning map forces Julia to choose which fact matters.
chapter_evidence.counterintuition: More information can make judgment worse when it arrives without a distinction. Thinking improves when facts become a usable choice.
chapter_evidence.takeaway: Better thinking turns information into distinctions, connections, and judgment instead of raw accumulation.
chapter_evidence.try: Before your next decision, write the distinction that would change the choice, then sort facts by whether they affect it.
extracts: Andrew reads a mock-trial transcript marked with colored sticky flags.
Thinking asks the facts to earn their place.
The facts that remain are fewer, sharper, and harder to evade.
examples: Julia Draws the Tradeoff on Tracing Paper
Pavel Separates Medical from Home on the Whiteboard
Beatrice Lays Three Price Cards on the Table
chapter_evidence.coreSkill: Convert information into a visible distinction before making a decision or recommendation. The skill is identifying what the choice actually turns on — the tradeoff, the column, the rival hypothesis — and making it explicit before adding more input.
chapter_evidence.challenge: Take one decision you have been deferring. Before reading one more source, draw the tradeoff on a blank page: what are the two sides and what would settle it? Then decide whether additional information is actually needed.
